en: Praśastapādabhāṣya: Auspicious Invocation 0.0: The Praśastapādabhāṣya.
1.1ab: Having bowed down before the Lord, the cause [of all], the sage Kaṇāda;
1.1cd: the compendium of the properties of categories (padārthadharmasaṃgraha), which leads to great exaltation, shall now be proclaimed.

2.1: The knowledge of the true nature of the six categories—substance, quality, action, generality, particularity, and inherence—through their similarities and differences, is the cause of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*).
2.1: And that [knowledge] arises solely from dharma manifested through the injunction of the Lord.
2.2: Now, what are the categories (padārtha) such as substance (dravya) and so forth, and what is their similarity (sādharmya) and dissimilarity (vaidharmya)?

2.2: Among those, the substances—earth, water, fire, air, ether, time, space, self, and mind—are said to be exactly nine by way of their general and specific designations; for no other designation is mentioned apart from them.

2.2: Qualities (guṇas) are seventeen as explicitly stated: color, taste, smell, touch, number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort. Furthermore, there are seven others—gravity, fluidity, viscidity, mental impression (saṃskāra), merit, demerit, and sound—which are included by the word "and" (ca). Thus, there are twenty-four qualities in total.

2.2: There are exactly five types of action: throwing upward, throwing downward, contraction, expansion, and locomotion. Because of the inclusion of "locomotion," whirling, evacuation, flowing, upward flaming, horizontal blowing, bending, and straightening are specific varieties of locomotion and do not constitute distinct classes.

2.2: Generality (*sāmānya*) is twofold: the higher (*para*) and the lower (*apara*), being the cause of the cognition of inclusion (*anuvṛtti*). Among these, the higher is existence (*sattā*), because its scope is vast; and since it is the cause of inclusion alone, it is generality only. The lower consists of [categories] such as substantiality (*dravyatva*), because their scope is limited. And since that [lower generality] is also the cause of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), while being a generality, it also receives the designation of "particular" (*viśeṣa*).
2.2: Ultimate particularities (antyaviśeṣas) reside in eternal substances. Indeed, they are called "particularities" alone because they are the cause of absolute differentiation.

2.2: Inherence (*samavāya*) is that relation between things that are inseparably established (*ayutasiddha*) and stand in the relationship of the supported and the support, which is the cause of the cognition "here [in this]."
2.2: Thus has the enumeration of the substrata (dharmin) been made without their properties (dharma).
2.3: All six categories possess existence, nameability, and knowability.
2.3: And [the property of] being dependent [belongs] to everything other than eternal substances.
2.3: The five categories beginning with substance possess the properties of inherence and plurality.
2.3: Regarding the five categories beginning with quality (guṇa), they are likewise devoid of qualities and devoid of action.

2.3: Furthermore, the three categories beginning with substance (dravya) possess a connection with existence (sattā), the quality of possessing generality and particularity (sāmānyaviśeṣavatva), being denotable by words whose meanings are established within their own system (svasamayārthaśabdābhidheyatva), and being the agents of merit and demerit (dharmādharmakartṛtva).
2.3: Being an effect and being impermanent belong only to those things that possess causes.
2.3: And causality [belongs] to all things except for spherical dimension and so forth.
2.3: And [the property of] being dependent on a substance exists in all things except for eternal substances.

2.3: The three categories beginning with generality (sāmānya) possess existence in their own right, are characterized by cognition, are neither effects nor causes, do not possess further generalities or particulars, are eternal, and are not denotable by the word "object" (artha).

3. Non-confusion of substances: the nine [substances], beginning with earth, possess the property of being a substance (*dravyatva*); they possess the quality of being initiators within themselves, the quality of possessing qualities (*guṇavattva*), the state of being opposed by their effects and causes, and the possession of ultimate particularities (*antyaviśeṣavattva*).
3: And [the properties of] non-dependence and permanence [belong] to things other than composite substances.
3: [The proof of] the multiplicity and possession of a lower genus (aparajāti) for earth, water, fire, air, self, and mind.
3: Earth, water, light, air, and mind possess the qualities of activity, corporeality, priority, posteriority, and velocity.
3: Space, time, direction, and the self possess omnipresence, supreme magnitude, and co-extensiveness with all conjoined entities.

3: All five elements, beginning with earth, possess the properties of being elemental substances (*bhūta*), being the material causes (*prakṛti*) of the sense organs, and possessing specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) that are perceptible by a single external sense organ.
3: The four [substances] possess the qualities of being initiators of substances and possessing touch.
3: The three possess perceptibility, possession of form, and fluidity.
3: The two possess gravity and flavor.
3: The elemental selves possess specific qualities.
3: Earth, water, and the self possess fourteen qualities.
3: The possession of particular qualities that are momentary and reside in only one part of those whose nature is space.
3: Space and time possess five qualities and serve as the efficient cause (nimittakāraṇa) for all things that originate.
3: Earth and fire possess occasional liquidity.
3: Thus, in all cases, similarity is to be stated through correspondence, and dissimilarity through its opposite; this constitutes the non-confusion of substances.
Vaidharmya 4.0: Now, the dissimilarity (vaidharmya) is stated for each [reason] individually.

4.1: [Earth] is earth because of its connection with the universal *pṛthivītva* (earthness). It possesses color, taste, smell, touch, number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, gravity, fluidity, and momentum (*saṃskāra*). These specific qualities, beginning with color, are established in the section on the "inclusion of qualities. From the mention of being "visible," the seven qualities beginning with number are established. From the teaching regarding falling, gravity is established. From the mention of having "commonality with water," substantiality (*dravyatva*) is established. From the mention of "subsequent action," momentum is established.

4.1: Odor exists only in earth. Color is of many kinds, such as white and so forth. Taste is of six kinds, beginning with sweet. Odor is of two kinds: fragrant and foul. Its touch, being neither hot nor cold, is produced by maturation (*pākaja*).

4.1: It (earth) is of two kinds: eternal and non-eternal. That which is characterized as atoms is eternal; that which is characterized as an effect, however, is non-eternal. And this [non-eternal earth] is distinguished by the arrangement of its parts, such as stability and so forth; it possesses a multiplicity of subordinate genera and provides manifold assistance, such as serving as beds, seats, and the like. Its effects are threefold, designated as body, sense organ, and object.

4.1: The body is of two kinds: born from a womb (*yonija*) and not born from a womb (*ayonija*). Among these, that which is not born from a womb arises for the gods and sages from atoms accompanied by a specific merit (*dharma*), independent of semen and blood. The bodies of tormented beings (*yātanā-śarīra*) for minute creatures arise from atoms accompanied by a specific demerit (*adharma*). That which is born from a womb arises from the union of semen and blood; it is twofold: viviparous (*jarāyuja*) and oviparous (*aṇḍaja*). The viviparous belong to humans, cattle, and wild animals; the oviparous belong to birds and reptiles.
4.1: The sense organ that manifests odors for all living beings is the olfactory organ (*ghrāṇa*), which is composed of earthy atoms not overwhelmed by water and the other elements.

As for its object, it is composed through the sequence beginning with dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and is of three kinds, characterized as earth, stone, and stationary (*sthāvara*). Among these, types of earth include regions of the ground, walls, bricks, and so forth; stones include rocks, gems, diamonds, and so forth; and stationary things include grasses, herbs, trees, shrubs, creepers, climbing plants, and forest trees.

4.2: Water is so called because of its connection with the quality of moisture (*āptva*). It possesses color, taste, touch, fluidity, viscidity, number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, weight, and faculty (*saṃskāra*). Their establishment is as before. Its color, taste, and touch are exclusively white, sweet, and cold. Viscidity and natural fluidity exist only in water.
4.2: These [waters] are also of two kinds, as before, because they exist as both eternal and non-eternal. Their effects, however, are threefold, designated as body, sense organ, and object.
Among these, the body is exclusively non-womb-born in the world of Varuṇa; and through the support of earthly particles, it becomes capable of experience.
The sense organ is the tongue, which manifests taste for all living beings and is composed of water-particles that are not overwhelmed by those of a different class.
4.2: The object, however, consists of rivers, oceans, snowflakes, and so forth.

4.3: It is fire because of its connection with the nature of fire (*tejastva*). It possesses color, touch, number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, fluidity, and faculty (*saṃskāra*).
4.3: Their establishment is as previously [explained].
4.3: In that regard, its color is white and luminous; its touch is exclusively hot.

4.3: That [subtle body] is also of two kinds, because of its existence as both atoms and effects. The effect consists of the triad beginning with the body. 4.3: The body is non-uterine (born of no womb) in the world of the sun; and due to the support of earthly particles, it is capable of experience. 4.3:
The sense organ is the eye, which manifests color-form for all living beings and is composed of fiery particles that are not overwhelmed by other particles.

4.3: That which is designated as "object" (*viṣaya*) is of four kinds: terrestrial (*bhauma*), celestial (*divya*), digestive (*audarya*), and mineral (*ākaraja*). Among these, the terrestrial arises from fuel such as wood and has the nature of upward flaming; it is capable of cooking, burning, and heating. The celestial does not have fuel as its substrate and consists of sunlight, lightning, and so forth. The digestive exists for the purpose of transforming the consumed food into chyle (*rasa*) and other constituents. The mineral consists of gold and the like.
In this regard, the perception of taste and other qualities occurs through inherence in that which is conjoined (*samyukta-samavāya*).

4.4: Air is that which is connected with the nature of air (*vāyutva*). It possesses touch, number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, and impression (*saṃskāra*). Its touch is established as being neither hot nor cold and not produced by heat (*apākaja*), due to its inclusion among the qualities [in the *Guṇasūtra*]. The seven qualities beginning with number are established because of the statement [in the *Guṇasūtra*] regarding "those lacking color are not visible. Impression is established because of the mention of the motion of grass [blown by wind]. Furthermore, this [air] is of two kinds, owing to its existence as both atomic (*aṇu*) and as an effect (*kārya*).
4.4: Among these, that characterized as an effect is fourfold: the body, the sense organ, the object, and the vital breath. 4.4:
Among these, the body of the Maruts is exclusively non-womb-born; it is capable of experience due to the support of earthly constituent parts. 4.4:

The sense organ is the tactile sense (tvag-indriya), which perceives touch for all living beings; it is composed of particles of air that are not overwhelmed by earth and the other elements, and it pervades the entire body.

4.4: The object [of touch], however, is that which serves as the substrate for the perceived touch; it has touch, sound, support, and motion as its marks (*liṅga*); its intrinsic nature is horizontal movement; and it is capable of impelling and supporting clouds and other such things. Although this [air] is not perceptible, its manifoldness is inferred through *sammūrcchana*. *Sammūrcchana*, moreover, is the collision of two winds of equal velocity moving in opposite directions. That [collision] is also inferred by the upward movement of two winds that possess parts; and that [upward movement] is inferred by the movement of grass and other such objects.

4.4: Prāṇa, being one, is the cause of the impelling and other functions of the bodily fluids, waste products, and constituent elements within the body; it receives the designations of apāna and so forth due to the differentiation of its activities.
The Procedure for Creation and Destruction 5: Now, here, the procedure for the creation and destruction of the four great elements is being stated.

5. At the end of a hundred years, according to the measurement of Brahmā, when Brahmā is about to attain liberation (*apavarga*), for the sake of providing rest during the night to all living beings exhausted by the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), at the very moment Maheśvara, the Lord of all worlds, desires to withdraw the universe, there occurs a cessation of the activity of the unseen forces (*adṛṣṭa*) residing in all selves—which are the causes that bind together the body, the sense organs, and the gross elements. Then, due to actions born from the conjunction of the will of Maheśvara with the selves and the atoms, and resulting in the disjunction of the atoms that are the causes of the bodies and sense organs, the conjunctions [of those atoms] cease; consequently, the destruction of those [bodies and organs] takes place down to the level of the individual atoms.

5: Likewise, among the great elements—earth, water, fire, and air—in this very same sequence, upon the existence of each subsequent one, there is the destruction of each preceding one; thereafter, the atoms remain distinct, permeated by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*), for that very duration of time.

5: Then again, for the sake of the enjoyment of living beings, immediately following Maheśvara’s desire to create, and depending upon the unseen merit and demerit (adṛṣṭa) residing in all souls which has attained its functional state, motion arises in the atoms of air due to their conjunctions with those [souls]. From the mutual conjunctions of these atoms, a great wind is produced through the process beginning with dyads (dvyaṇuka), and it remains vibrating in the sky.

5: Immediately thereafter, from those very atoms of air, in that same sequence, a great ocean is produced; it remains floating about. Immediately thereafter, from those very atoms of earth, the great earth remains as a solid mass. Immediately thereafter, within that very great ocean, from atoms of fire, a great mass of light is produced through the process beginning with dyads (dvyaṇuka) and so forth; it remains blazing intensely because it cannot be overcome by anything else.

5: Thus, when the four great elements have arisen, by the mere volition of Maheśvara, a great egg (aṇḍa) is produced from fiery atoms conjoined with earthly atoms; and having produced within it Brahmā—the lotus-face of the four-faced one, the grandfather of all worlds—along with the entire universe, he appoints him to the creation of living beings.

And he, commissioned by Maheśvara, endowed with supreme knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty regarding Brahman, having understood the ripening of the karma of living beings, created from his mind the Prajāpatis, the sons [of Brahmā] whose knowledge, enjoyments, and lifespans correspond to their respective karmas; and having created the four castes from his mouth, arms, thighs, and feet, as well as other high and low beings, he endows them with virtue, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty according to their latent dispositions (*āśaya*).

6.1 Substance as a Category: Since ether, time, and space are each singular, there being no higher genus for them, they possess three technical designations: ether (*ākāśa*), time (*kāla*), and space (*diś*). Among these, the qualities of ether are sound, number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, and disjunction.

6.1: Sound is not a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of tangible substances (*sparśavat*), because it does not presuppose the qualities of its causes, because it does not persist as long as the substance exists, and because it is perceived elsewhere than in its substratum. It is not a quality of the self (*ātman*), because it is perceptible by an external sense organ, because it can be apprehended by another person, because it does not inhere in the self, and because it is perceived as distinct from the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*). It does not belong to space, time, or the internal organ (*manas*), because it is apprehended by the auditory organ and because it lacks the status of a specific quality [of those]. By process of elimination, being a quality, it is the probans (*liṅga*) for the cognition of space. Its oneness is established because there is no difference in the probans, namely sound.

6.1: From its conformity [to space], it has the singularity of being one; from the statement regarding its pervasiveness, it has the dimension of supreme magnitude (*paramamahat-parimāṇa*); and from the statement regarding its being the cause of sound, it possesses conjunction and disjunction. Therefore, because it possesses qualities and because it is not dependent [on anything else], it is a substance (*dravya*). Furthermore, because it lacks causes of either a similar or dissimilar kind, it is eternal. And it serves as the instrumental cause for all living beings in the perception of sound by way of being the auditory organ (*śrotra*).

6.1: Furthermore, the auditory organ (*śrotra*) is a region of space (*nabhodeśa*) characterized by the cavity of the ear, which is bound by merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) that bring about the experience of sound as its cause; and since it is eternal, deafness occurs due to the deficiency of that which binds it.

6.2: Time is characterized by the notions of priority and posteriority, simultaneity and non-simultaneity, slowness and quickness. Since there is no other cause for the arising of those notions—which are distinct from previous notions regarding their respective objects—that which is the cause therein is time. Furthermore, it is the cause of the production, persistence, and destruction of all effects, as designated by such terms; it is the basis for the conventional usage of moments (*kṣaṇa*), instants (*lava*), winks (*nimeṣa*), *kāṣṭhā*, *kalā*, *muhūrta*, watches (*yāma*), days and nights, fortnights, months, seasons, solstices (*ayana*), years, *yuga* cycles, *kalpa* periods, intermediate *manvantara* periods, dissolution (*pralaya*), and the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*).

6.2: Its qualities are number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, and disjunction. Oneness is established because the marks of time are non-distinct. Distinctness follows from that [oneness]. The dimension of infinite magnitude is established by the statement "time is a cause. Conjunction is established by the statement regarding "priority" and so forth, which depend on a cause.

6.2: Disjunction (*vibhāga*) is so called because it causes the destruction of that [conjunction]. Since its status as a substance and its eternity are established—just like space—and since it is unitary by nature due to the non-distinction of its defining marks (*liṅga*) from those of time, the metaphorical designation of multiplicity is applied to it, as in the case of a jewel or a cook, owing to the distinctions among the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) consisting of the commencement, accomplishment, maintenance, and cessation of all effects.

6.3: Space (*dik*) is characterized by the notions of "east," "west," and so forth. Taking a corporeal substance as a limit, it is that from which there arise these ten notions regarding corporeal substances alone—namely, "this is to the east," "to the south," "to the west," "to the north," "to the southeast," "to the southwest," "to the northwest," "to the northeast," "below," and "above"—and no other cause for these is possible. Therefore, it is space. 6.3: Because no other cause is possible.

6.3: Its qualities—number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, and disjunction—are established as being like those of time. Since the indicative marks of direction are non-distinct, direction is essentially one; nevertheless, for the sake of worldly convention according to the Vedas, the Smṛtis, and common usage, the venerable great seers have assigned ten conventional designations—East and so forth—to the specific conjunctions of the divine Sun as he revolves clockwise around Meru, corresponding to the regions of space presided over by the world-protectors. Thus, metaphorically, the ten directions are established.

6.3: Due to their being presided over by these very deities, they further possess ten designations: namely, the Māhendrī, Vaiśvānarī, Yāmyā, Nairṛtī, Vāruṇī, Vāyavyā, Kauverī, Aiśānī, Brāhmī, and Nāgī.

6.4: It is called the *ātman* because of its connection with the nature of self. Since it is not perceptible due to its subtlety, it is apprehended through the instruments—the ears and so forth—which are inferred from the perception of sound and other objects. Because instruments such as axes are seen to be employed by an agent, and because of the well-known application [of this principle] to sound and the rest, that which accomplishes [the perception] is inferred.

6.4: [Consciousness does not belong] to the body, the senses, or the mind, because they are insentient. Consciousness does not belong to the body, because it is an effect of the elements like a jar and because it is impossible in a dead person. It does not belong to the senses, because they are instruments and because we observe the recollection of objects even when the senses are impaired or the objects are absent.

6.4: Nor can it be the mind, because if the mind were independent of other instruments, there would be the consequence of simultaneous perception and memory, and because the mind itself lacks the status of an instrument. By process of elimination, since [pleasure and pain] are effects of the self, the self is thereby established. Furthermore, by means of activity and cessation—which inhere in the body and are capable of attaining the beneficial and avoiding the harmful—the self is inferred as the conscious controller of the body, like a charioteer of a chariot; and it is also [established] by means of the vital breaths and so forth.

6.4: How [is it known that there is a self]? Because when the wind is contained within the body, one observes modified actions—such as the regular action of closing and opening the eyes like a person blowing a bellows—and because [the body] serves as the cause for growth, the healing of wounds, the mending of fractures, and so forth, like a person operating a wooden machine.

6.4: Just as a householder is known by his activity of mind—which, caused by the connection with the instruments that grasp desired objects—acts like a child throwing a ball in the corners of a house; and because a modification of the sense of taste is observed following the perception of a visual object through a sequence of recollecting its flavor; thus, like a spectator looking through many windows, a single entity is discerned who perceives both.

6.4: The possessor of qualities (guṇin) is inferred from the qualities of pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort; and these [qualities] are not qualities of the body or the sense organs. Why? Because they do not form a single syntactical unit with the notion of "I" (ahaṅkāra), because they exist only in specific locations, because they do not persist as long as the substance itself, and because they are not perceptible by the external senses; likewise, because the word "I" is distinct from words such as "divine" and so forth.

6.4: Its qualities are cognition (*buddhi*), pleasure (*sukha*), pain (*duḥkha*), desire (*icchā*), aversion (*dveṣa*), volition (*prayatna*), merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), mental impression (*saṃskāra*), number (*saṃkhyā*), dimension (*parimāṇa*), distinctness (*pṛthaktva*), conjunction (*saṃyoga*), and disjunction (*vibhāga*). In the section concerning the marks of the self (*ātmaliṅga*), those beginning with cognition and ending with volition are established. Merit and demerit are established because it is stated that they are not causes for the qualities of other selves. Mental impression is established because it is stated to be the cause for the arising of memory. Number is established because of the statement regarding its specific distribution; distinctness is likewise established for the same reason. Furthermore, from the statement "and thus the self," its dimension is that of the supreme magnitude (*paramamahat*).
6.4: Because pleasure and the like arise from proximity (*sannikarṣa*), [the cause] is conjunction (*saṃyoga*); because it destroys them, it is disjunction (*vibhāga*).

6.5: It is called *manas* because of its connection with the nature of mind (*manastva*). Even when the self, the senses, and their objects are present, since we observe that cognition, pleasure, and so forth arise after having not previously existed, another instrument (*karaṇa*) is inferred. Because memory is observed to arise even when the ear and other [senses] are inactive, and because there exists another object of perception such as pleasure which is not grasped by the external senses, it is the internal organ (*antahkaraṇa*).

6.5: Its qualities are number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, and mental impression (*saṃskāra*). From the statement regarding the non-simultaneity of effort and cognition, its oneness in each body is established. Distinctness is also established for this very reason. From the statement regarding its absence [of magnitude], it possesses atomic dimension. From the mention of "receding" and "approaching," it possesses conjunction and disjunction. Because it is corporeal, it possesses priority, posteriority, and mental impression. Because it lacks touch, it does not originate substances. Because it possesses motion, it is corporeal. Because it would entail having a common physical form, it is devoid of consciousness.

6.5: It exists for the sake of another because it is an instrument; it is a substance because it possesses qualities; and it moves swiftly by virtue of being seized by effort and the unseen force (adṛṣṭa).
6.0: Thus ends the category of substance (dravyapadārtha) in the Praśastapādabhāṣya.
The Definition of the Category of Quality (Guṇapadārtha):
Now follows the definition of the category of quality.

All qualities, such as color and the rest, are characterized by their connection with the universal "quality-ness" (guṇatva), their dependence upon substance (dravyāśritatva), their lack of further qualities (nirguṇatva), and their lack of action (niṣkriyatva).

7.0: Conjunction, disjunction, duality, double separateness, and so forth, are dependent upon multiple substrates.
7.0: But the remaining [qualities] reside in each individual substance.

The category of quality (guṇapadārtha):
8.1: Because each of all the qualities, such as color-form and so forth, is connected with its own particular generality (aparasāmānya), they receive the designations "color-form" and so on.

8.1: Among these, color (*rūpa*) is that which is grasped by the eye; it subsists in earth, water, and fire; it is the means of perceiving substances and so forth; it assists the eye [in its function]; it is of many kinds, such as white and others; it is eternal in the atoms of water and so forth; it is opposed to contact with fire in the atoms of earth; in all produced substances, it is preceded by the qualities of its causes; and it perishes solely through the destruction of its substratum.

8.2: Taste is that which is apprehended by the sense of taste. It resides in earth and water; it is the cause of life, nourishment, strength, and health; it assists the sense of taste; and it is divided into the distinctions of sweet, sour, salty, bitter, pungent, and astringent. Its eternality, non-eternality, and production are like those of color.

8.3: Odor is that which is apprehended by the sense of smell; it resides in earth, acts as an auxiliary to the sense of smell, and is either fragrant or foul. Its production and other characteristics are explained as before.

8.4: Touch is that which is apprehended by the sense organ of the skin. It resides in earth, water, fire, and air; it enables the perception of the skin; it conforms to color; and it is of three kinds, distinguished as cold, hot, and neither-hot-nor-cold. Its eternity, non-eternity, and production are also as previously described.

8.5: The process of the production of qualities such as color arising from heating (*pākaja*) in the case of earth-atoms (*pārthivaparamāṇu*). When a raw substance such as a jar is in contact with fire, actions arise in the atoms that constitute it, either due to the impact of the fire or due to its impulsion. From these [actions] come disjunctions; from the disjunctions, the destruction of conjunctions; and from the destruction of conjunctions, the effect-substance perishes. When that has perished, in the independent atoms, the destruction of blackness and other qualities occurs through the conjunction with fire, depending on heat. Then, from another conjunction with fire, depending on heat, the qualities produced by heating (*pākaja*) arise.

8.5: Immediately thereafter, due to the conjunction of the self and the atoms—dependent upon the unseen merit or demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) of the experiencers—action arises in the atoms in which qualities produced by heating (*pākaja*) have been generated. From the mutual conjunction of these atoms, the effect-substance (*kāryadravya*) is produced through the sequence beginning with the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*). In that process, the production of color and other qualities occurs according to the sequence of the qualities of the causes.

Furthermore, the production or destruction of color and other qualities cannot occur in the effect-substance itself [prior to its formation], because fire lacks the capacity to pervade it both internally and externally across all its constituent parts; nor can pervasion occur even through the entry of minute particles, since the effect-substance would have already been destroyed [by the time such entry could occur].

8.6: Number (*saṃkhyā*) is the cause for the conventional usage of "one" and so forth. It is further divided into that which resides in a single substance (*ekadravyā*) and that which resides in multiple substances (*anekadravyā*). Among these, regarding the number residing in a single substance—such as the form of water-atoms and the like—their eternity, non-eternity, and production are [to be understood] just as those of the atoms themselves. However, the number residing in multiple substances begins with duality (*dvitva*) and ends with the highest unit (*parārdha*). The production of this [number] occurs from unities (*ekatva*) accompanied by a cognition of multiple objects; its destruction occurs through the destruction of the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*). How so?

8.6: When, upon the contact of the observer's eye with two substances—one of the same class and one of a different class—there arises the cognition of the generality of unity (*ekatvasāmānya*) inherent in that which is inherent in what is conjoined (*tatsaṃyuktasamavetasamaveta*), then, from the cognition of the generality of unity and from the cognitions of the relations [of inherence], there arises a single cognition directed toward multiple objects regarding two unities. At that time, with reference to that [cognition], duality is initiated in the two things which are its own substrates. Thereafter, the cognition of the generality of duality arises in respect to that [duality]. From that cognition of the generality of duality, the state of the non-perishing (*vinaśyattā*) of the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) occurs; and simultaneously, from the generality of duality, its relation, and the cognition thereof, the cognition of the quality of duality begins to arise. This constitutes one moment of time.

8.6: Then, at this point, due to the destruction of the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), there is the state of the quality of duality being about to perish; the cognition of the quality of duality is the cause of the destruction of the cognition of the generality of duality; and from the relation between the quality of duality and its cognition, the cognition of the substance "two substances" is arising—these constitute one single moment.

8.6: Immediately after that, there is the arising of the cognition of the two substances (*dravyajñāna*), the destruction of duality (*dvitva*), the state of the cognition of the quality of duality being about to perish, and the state of the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) being produced from the cognition of the substances—this constitutes one single moment. Immediately after that, from the cognition of the substances, there is the destruction of the cognition of the quality of duality, and also the destruction of the cognition of the substances themselves from the mental impression. By this, the production of triad (*tritva*) and so forth is also explained: their production arises from the unitary natures (*ekatva*) accompanied by the cognition of multiple objects, and their destruction arises from the destruction of the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*). In some cases, however, it is due to the destruction of the substratum (*āśraya*). How so?

8.6: When action arises in a constituent part that is the substratum of unity, at that very same time the cognition of the generality of unity arises; by means of that action, disjunction from another part is produced, and there is the arising of relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*). Then, at the very same time that the destruction of conjunction occurs due to that disjunction, duality (*dvitva*) arises; from the destruction of conjunction follows the destruction of the substance, and there is the arising of the cognition of the generality [of duality].

8.6: Therefore, at the very moment when the destruction of the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) occurs due to the destruction of its common substrate, at that same moment the destruction of duality (*dvitva*) occurs due to the destruction of its substratum. This formulation is excellent [in the case of] the "slayer and slain" position; however, if there were opposition characterized by non-coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*), it would follow that no cognition of the substance could ever arise. How so?

8.6: Since the destruction of duality occurs simultaneously with the destruction of the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) due to the cognition of the quality, there would follow the undesirable consequence that the cognition of the substance—namely, "two substances"—which depends upon that [duality], would not arise. If it is argued that this is like inferential knowledge (*laiṅgika*), such that "from mere cognition," [the object is known]—meaning, as in the case of "the past from what has not yet occurred," where inference proceeds from mere cognition even in the absence of a logical mark (*liṅga*)—then likewise, even upon the destruction of the quality, the perception of the substance would occur from the mere cognition of the quality.

8.6: No, because [the cognition] is a cognition of a qualified object (*viśeṣya*). For a cognition of a qualified object cannot arise through similarity without a connection to a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). Thus the author of the Sūtras says: "From the whiteness inherent [in the substance], there arises the cognition of whiteness; from that [cognition of whiteness], there arises the cognition of the white [substance]; these two stand in the relation of cause and effect. But inferential cognition does not arise without [perceiving] the distinction [between the mark and the possessor of the mark]; therefore, this comparison is unequal. [Objection: It is not so, because of rapid production. Just as in the case of "Space possesses sound," three cognitions arise rapidly, so too it is in the production of the cognition of duality and so forth; thus there is no fault.

8.6: If it be thought that the same fault applies even in the case of the "slayer and the slain" (badhyaghātaka) theory, [we reply: indeed, in that case too, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that the cognition of the substance does not arise. How so? Because at the very moment of the cognition of the generality of duality, the relative cognition (apekṣābuddhi) is destroyed by the latent impression (saṃskāra). [We reply: No.

8.6: Since collective cognition (*samūhajñāna*) is the cause of the mental impression (*saṃskāra*), it is collective cognition alone that is the cause of the impression, not the initial sensory perception (*ālocanajñāna*); thus there is no fault. If it be argued that this leads to the undesirable consequence of the simultaneity of cognitions (*jñānayaugapadyaprasaṅga*)—for surely, if cognitions are in a relationship of mutual destruction (*badhyaghātaka*), it would entail their simultaneity—we say:
no, because we deny the coexistence of two [cognitions] that do not perish.

8.6: By the statement regarding the non-simultaneity of cognitions, the simultaneous arising of two cognitions and the simultaneous persistence of two [cognitions] that have not yet perished are both prohibited; for in the case of the contradiction between the bound and the slayer, there is neither the simultaneous arising of two cognitions nor the simultaneous persistence of two [cognitions] that are perishing.

8.7: Dimension (*parimāṇa*) is the cause for the conventional usage of measurement. It is fourfold: minute (*aṇu*), large (*mahat*), long (*dīrgha*), and short (*hrasva*). Among these, the large is of two kinds: eternal (*nitya*) and non-eternal (*anitya*). The eternal [large dimension] is the supreme largeness (*paramamahattva*) existing in space (*ākāśa*), time (*kāla*), direction (*diś*), and the self (*ātman*); the non-eternal exists only in triads (*tryaṇuka*) and so forth.

8.7: Likewise, even the minute (*aṇu*) is of two kinds: eternal and non-eternal. The eternal [minute] is the spherical dimension (*pārimāṇḍalya*) found in atoms and the internal organs (*manas*). The non-eternal [minute] exists only in the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*). Even in large objects such as the *kuvalaya*, *āmalaka*, and *bilva* fruits, the conventional usage of "minuteness" is figurative, depending on the presence or absence of the excellence of that [spherical dimension]. Length (*dīrghatva*) and shortness (*hrasvatva*), moreover, are produced and are inherent in the same substratum as largeness and minuteness. Even in things like sacrificial fuel sticks, sugarcane, and bamboo which are directly long, the conventional usage of "shortness" is figurative, depending on the presence or absence of the excellence of that [length].

8.7: Impermanence is fourfold, having its origin in number (*saṃkhyā*), dimension (*parimāṇa*), and aggregation (*pracaya*). Among these, the number "plurality" (*bahutva*) produced in dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) by depending upon the intellect of God (*īśvara-buddhi*) produces both largeness (*mahattva*) and length (*dīrghatva*) simultaneously with the production of color and other qualities in the effect-substance characterized as a triad (*tryaṇuka*) and so forth, which is initiated by those [dyads].

In an effect-substance initiated by two or many large [causes], it is the dimensions of the causes themselves that initiate largeness, not plurality; for even when initiated by causes of equal number, a superior degree [of size] is observed.

8.7: Largeness (*mahattva*) residing in two cotton-balls (*tūlapiṇḍa*) initiates largeness in the double-cotton-ball (*dvitūlaka*), depending either on the loose conjunctions of the constituent parts that initiate the balls, or on the mutual conjunctions of the parts of the two balls; it does not depend on plurality (*bahutva*) or [other instances of] largeness. This is because an excess [of size] is observed in what is produced by parts possessing an equal number and weight. Furthermore, duality (*dvitvasaṃkhyā*) residing in two atoms initiates minuteness (*aṇutva*) in the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*). Just like largeness, length (*dīrghatva*) arises in the triad (*tryaṇuka*) and so forth from plurality, largeness, and homogeneous accumulation (*pracaya*) of causes.

8.7: Just as minuteness arises in a dyad from the number two, so too does shortness arise [therefrom]. Now, regarding the largeness and length residing in triads and the like, what is the distinction between them, and likewise, what is the distinction between minuteness and shortness in dyads?

8.7: In that regard, there is a mutual distinction between largeness and length, because we observe specific linguistic usage such as, "Let the long one be brought from among the large," and "Let the large one be brought from among the long."

8.7: Furthermore, the distinction between atomicity (*aṇutva*) and shortness (*hrasvatva*) is perceptible to those who perceive it. Moreover, all four kinds of dimension (*parimāṇa*), being produced, perish solely through the destruction of their substratum.

8.8: Separateness (*pṛthaktva*) is the cause for the linguistic usage of distinction. It resides in a single substance as well as in multiple substances. Its eternality, non-eternality, and production have been explained by analogy with number (*saṃkhyā*). However, there is this distinction: unlike unity and so forth, there is no lower universal (*aparasāmānya*) within singular separateness and so on; rather, it is distinguished by number, because we observe that linguistic usage is qualified by it.

8.9: Conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is the cause of the cognition of "conjoined. It is also the cause of substances, qualities, and actions. Regarding the initiation of a substance, it functions independently, according to the statement: "[A substance arises] from those that are dependent and from those that are independent. However, regarding the initiation of a quality or an action, it is dependent [on other causes], according to the statement: "The specific quality of fire [arises] from conjunction with that which is inherent (*saṃyuktasamavāya*)."

8.9: Now, what are its characteristics and how many kinds are there? Conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is the reaching together of two things that were previously unjoined; it is of three kinds: produced by the action of one, produced by the action of both, and produced by conjunction. Among these, that produced by the action of one is the [conjunction] of an inactive object with an active one, such as that of a post with a hawk, or of all-pervading substances (*vibhu*) with corporeal objects (*mūrta*). That produced by the action of both is the meeting of two things possessing actions in opposite directions, such as that of two wrestlers or two rams.

8.9: Conjunction produced by conjunction (*samyogaja*), however, is a conjunction occurring between an effect and a non-effect, preceded by a conjunction between a cause and a non-cause; it belongs to that which has just arisen or that which has arisen long ago and is currently devoid of motion, and it occurs through causes that are themselves conjoined with [other] non-causes. Furthermore, it arises from one, from two, or from many. First, from one: from the conjunction of a thread and a *vīraṇa* grass, there arises a conjunction of a two-threaded fabric (*dvitantuka*) and a *vīraṇa* grass. From two: from two conjunctions of a thread and space, there arises a single conjunction of a two-threaded fabric and space. And from many: from many conjunctions of threads and a shuttle (*tūrī*), there arises a single conjunction of a cloth (*paṭa*) and a shuttle.

8.9: And the production of two [dyads] from one [atom]. How so? When there is a conjunction of an earth atom and a water atom, and simultaneously another conjunction occurs—of the earth atom with another earth atom and of the water atom with another water atom—then by means of those two conjunctions, two dyads consisting of earth and water are produced simultaneously.

8.9: Then, at the very time when the production of color and other qualities occurs in the two dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) through the sequence beginning with the qualities of the causes, at that same time, from the conjunction residing in each respective cause and non-cause, two conjunctions residing in each respective effect and non-effect are produced simultaneously. Why is this?

Because there is a logical rule (*nyāya*) that an effect must necessarily be conjoined with a non-cause that is conjoined with its own cause; therefore, the earth dyad is connected with the water atom which is conjoined with its own cause, and the water dyad is likewise connected with the earth atom which is conjoined with its own cause.

8.9: Now, how is there a mutual connection between two dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) that are themselves connected to their respective causes and non-causes? Their connection also occurs through two conjunctions produced by conjunction (*saṃyogaja-saṃyoga*). There is no eternal conjunction, because it is not mentioned separately [from the other types], just like the eternal spherical dimension (*parimaṇḍala*). Just as, after stating that the four kinds of dimension are produced, one says "the spherical is eternal," so too, after stating that conjunctions such as those produced by the action of one of two things are produced, one would have to state separately that there is an eternal [conjunction]; but he did not say this. Therefore, there is no eternal conjunction.

8.9: The partial inherence of ether and the other [substances] in atoms is due to conjunction produced by the action of one or the other. However, there is no mutual conjunction among all-pervading substances (*vibhu*), because they lack separate existence (*yutasiddhi*). This [separate existence] consists in either both or one of two things possessing distinct motions, or having distinct substrates. The destruction of every conjunction, however, occurs through disjunction inhering in the same object as the conjunction; in some cases, it also occurs through the destruction of the substrate. How so?

8.9: When, upon the conjunction of two threads, a motion arises in one of the constituent parts (*aṃśu*) that initiates the thread, by that motion a disjunction from the other part is produced; from that disjunction follows the destruction of the conjunction that initiated the thread; from the destruction of the conjunction follows the destruction of the thread; and upon its destruction, there is the destruction of the conjunction with the other thread which was dependent upon it.

8.10: Disjunction (vibhāga) is the cause of the cognition of separation; it is also the cause of the separation of sounds. Disjunction is non-attainment preceded by attainment. It is of three kinds: disjunction produced by the action of one [of two things], disjunction produced by the action of both, and disjunction produced by another disjunction.

8.10: Among these, those produced by the action of one [substance] and those produced by the actions of both are like conjunction (*saṃyoga*). However, that which is produced by disjunction (*vibhāga*) is of two kinds: from the disjunction of causes and from the disjunction of the cause and the non-cause. Regarding the first, concerning the cause occupied by the effect, it is a fixed principle that when an action arises in it, it effects a disjunction from another part of itself but not from a location such as space; whereas when it effects a disjunction from a location such as space, it does not [at that time] effect a disjunction from another part of itself.

8.10: Therefore, the action of a part initiates a disjunction from another part; from that disjunction follows the destruction of the conjunction that originates the substance. When that [conjunction] has perished, there is an absence of the effect due to the absence of its cause, and thus the destruction of the whole occurs. At that time, the disjunction residing in the two causes—depending either on the time characterized by the destruction of the effect or on the independent part itself—initiates a disjunction of the very active part from a location such as space (ākāśa) that was conjoined with the effect, but not of an inactive part, because of the absence of a cause; for if a subsequent conjunction were not produced, there would be the undesirable consequence of the part being incapable of being experienced. However, that action of the part does not produce a disjunction from space and so forth, because the time for its initiation has already passed; yet it certainly produces a conjunction with another location, since there is no lapse of time for an action that has not yet produced its conjunction.

8.10: How [is disjunction produced] even from the disjunction between the cause and the non-cause? When an action has arisen in the hand and, without producing a disjunction from another part [of the body], initiates disjunctions from locations such as space, it then initiates conjunctions with other locations; at that time, those disjunctions between the cause and the non-cause, with reference to whichever direction the action is oriented toward for the commencement of its effect, initiate disjunctions between the effect and the non-effect. Immediately thereafter, from the conjunction between the cause and the non-cause, they [initiate] conjunctions between the effect and the non-effect.

8.10: If it is argued that "if the production of the disjunction of the effect follows immediately after the disjunction of the cause, and the production of the conjunction of the effect follows immediately after the conjunction of the cause, then surely this entails the fault of the separate existence (*yutasiddhi*) of the part and the whole," we say: no, because there is a misunderstanding of what constitutes separate existence. That [separate existence] consists in the possession of distinct motions by two things, or by one of them; however, for eternal things, it is the inherence in separate substrata, whereas for non-eternal things, separate existence is defined as inherence in substrata that are themselves separate.

8.10: Since the sense-organ of touch and the body do not possess separate motions, their conjunction is established by the fact that there is inherence (*samavāya*) in their distinct substrates. However, in the case of an atom (*aṇu*) and space (*ākāśa*), even though there is no other substrate, conjunction and disjunction are established because one of the two possesses separate motion. Furthermore, since the threads and the cloth are non-eternal and lack another substrate, there is an absence of mutual conjunction and disjunction between them. As for direction (*dik*) and the other [categories], since they lack separate motion, there is an absence of mutual conjunction and disjunction.

8.10: However, the destruction of every disjunction is momentary because it has a subsequent conjunction as its limit; thus, it is momentary. But disjunction does not belong only to conjunction and cognition, for their destruction occurs through the very conjunction of those two. Why? Because, unlike the cognition of being conjoined, there is no persistence of a cognition of being disjoined [after the fact]. Therefore, because it has a subsequent conjunction as its limit, it is momentary. In some cases, however, it is destroyed simply by the destruction of its substratum. How so?

8.10: When an action has arisen in a fiber (aṃśu), which is a causal part of a two-threaded [cloth], and it initiates a disjunction from another fiber, at that very same time an action also arises in the other thread; and from that disjunction, the destruction of the conjunction that originated the thread occurs; and by the action of the thread, a disjunction from the other thread is produced—this constitutes one moment of time.

8.10: Then, at the very same time that the destruction of the conjunction of the threads occurs due to disjunction, at that same time, from the destruction of the conjunction, there is the destruction of the thread; when that [thread] has been destroyed, there is the destruction of the disjunction from the other thread which was dependent upon it. If this were so, it would follow as an undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that no subsequent disjunction could arise, because of the absence of a disjunction from a cause. Consequently, since there would be an absence of conjunction in that which already possesses a conjunction with another location, action would persist for a long duration due to the impossibility of a contrary quality (*virodhiguṇa*). Furthermore, there would be the fault that action inherent in an eternal substance would itself be eternal. How so?

8.10: When an action has arisen in a primary atom that initiates a dyad, it simultaneously produces a disjunction from another atom; at that very same time, an action also arises in that other atom. Then, at the same moment that the destruction of the conjunction initiating the substance occurs due to the disjunction, a disjunction between the dyad and the atom is produced by the action in the other atom. Then, at the very moment that the destruction of the conjunction between the dyad and the atom occurs due to the disjunction, the destruction of the dyad occurs due to the destruction of that conjunction.

8.10: When that [conjunction] has perished, there follows the destruction of the disjunction between the dyad and the atom which was dependent upon it; consequently, because a contrary quality cannot exist, action inhering in an eternal substance is eternal. [Objection: There is no fault here, for the disjunction [of the thread from the part] arises from the disjunction of the thread from another part. Due to the destruction of the substratum, the disjunction of the two threads themselves is destroyed, but the disjunction of the thread from the other part is not; from this, the subsequent disjunction is produced, just as the disjunction of the body from space arises from the disjunction of a finger from space. At that very same time, the action, having effected a conjunction, perishes; thus, there is no fault.

8.10: Alternatively, at the same time that the disjunction from another part arises, an action is produced in that very thread; then, from the disjunction from the other part, the destruction of the conjunction that originated the thread occurs, and by the action of the thread, a disjunction from the other thread is produced—this constitutes one moment of time.

8.10: Then, from the destruction of the conjunction follows the destruction of the thread; and from that destruction follows the simultaneous destruction of the disjunction and the action residing therein. Alternatively, when there is a conjunction between the thread and the *vīraṇa* grass, and no substance is produced, the destruction of the disjunction between the thread and the *vīraṇa* occurs through both the destruction of the substratum and the [destruction of the] conjunction, according to the method previously stated.

8.11: Remoteness (*paratva*) and proximity (*aparatva*) are the causes for the designations and cognitions of "remote" and "proximate. These are of two kinds: those produced by space (*dikkṛta*) and those produced by time (*kālakṛta*). Among these, that produced by space indicates a particular direction.

8.11: That produced by time (*kālakṛta*) is the indicator of the distinction in age. In this context, the production of that produced by space (*dikkṛta*) is now described. How so? When two objects are situated in the same direction, and there is a difference in the number of conjunctions with the points of contact [between them and the observer], an observer, taking one as the proximate limit, forms the cognition "this is remote from that" regarding the substratum of priority (*paratva*), which is the non-proximate object.

8.11: Then, by depending on that [object], through conjunction with a more distant spatial region (*dikpradeśa*), there arises the production of "remoteness" (*paratva*). Likewise, taking a distant object as the limit, the cognition "this is near to that" arises in the other object, which is the substratum of "nearness" (*aparatva*).
Then, by depending on that [cognition], through conjunction with a nearer spatial region, there arises the production of "nearness. How does this apply to those produced by time (*kāla*)?

8.11: When two persons, a young man and an old man, who exist at the present time and are connected to indefinite directions and locations, possess the presence of such qualities as grown facial hair, coarseness, wrinkles, and grey hair, a single observer forms the notion of "remoteness" with respect to the old man by taking the young man as the limit (*avadhi*). Then, through conjunction with a subsequent point in time and space relative to that [notion], there arises the production of "priority" (*paratva*). Furthermore, by taking the old man as the limit, the notion of "nearness" arises with respect to the young man; then, through conjunction with a preceding point in time and space relative to that [notion], there arises the production of "posteriority" (*aparatva*).

8.11: But destruction [of distance] results from the destruction of the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), the conjunction, and the substance. First, regarding destruction by the destruction of the relative cognition: at the time when the cognition of the universal (*sāmānyabuddhi*) has arisen once "priority" (*paratva*) has been produced, then there is the state of the relative cognition being about to perish; and simultaneously, there is the state of the cognition of the quality of priority (*paratvaguṇabuddhi*) being about to arise from the cognition of the universal, its relation [to the mind], and so forth. This constitutes one single moment.

8.11: Then, there is the destruction of the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) and the arising of the cognition of the quality (*guṇabuddhi*). Following that, from the destruction of the relative cognition, the quality enters a state of being destroyed; simultaneously, from the cognition of the quality, its relation [to the substance], and the substance itself, the cognition of the substance (*dravyabuddhi*) arises—this constitutes one moment. Subsequently, there is the arising of the cognition of the substance and the destruction of the quality. How does it occur through the destruction of conjunction (*saṃyogavināśa*) as well? At the very same time as the relative cognition, an action (*karman*) arises in the substratum of "priority" (*paratva*); by that action, a disjunction (*vibhāga*) between the direction (*dik*) and the object (*piṇḍa*) is produced. Simultaneously with the relative cognition, the priority (*paratva*) arises—this constitutes one moment.

8.11: From that, there arises the cognition of generality and the destruction of the conjunction between the direction and the substance. Then, at the very time when the cognition of the quality arises, at that same time, the destruction of the quality occurs due to the destruction of the conjunction between the direction and the substance. How also [does it occur] from the destruction of the substance?

8.11: When action arises in a constituent part that serves as the substratum for "remoteness" (paratva), at the very same time that it produces disjunction from another constituent part, the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) arises. Then, at the very time when the destruction of conjunction occurs due to that disjunction, remoteness (*paratva*) arises. Subsequently, from the destruction of conjunction comes the destruction of the substance; and from its destruction comes the destruction of the quality (*guṇa*) that was dependent upon it.

8.11: How [is this possible] even due to the simultaneous destruction of the substance and the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*)? At the very time when motion arises in a part of the substratum of "remoteness" (*paratva*), at that same time the relative cognition arises; and by that motion, a disjunction from another part is produced and the origination of "remoteness" occurs—this is one single moment.

8.11: Then, at the very moment when the destruction of the conjunction that initiates the substance occurs due to the separation of its parts, at that same moment the cognition of the universal (*sāmānya*) arises. Immediately thereafter, from the destruction of the conjunction comes the destruction of the substance, and from the cognition of the universal comes the destruction of the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*); thus, these occur at one and the same time. Subsequently, from the destruction of both the substance and the relative cognition, there is the destruction of "priority" (*paratva*). How also [does it occur] from the destruction of the conjunction with the substance?

8.11: When an action produced in a part that serves as the substratum for "remoteness" (paratva) effects a disjunction from another part, at that very same time, there is the simultaneous production of the action in the whole (piṇḍa) and the relative cognition (apekṣābuddhi). Then, at the very time that "remoteness" arises, at that same time, through the disjunction [caused by the action], the destruction of the conjunction that initiates the substance occurs; and by means of the action in the whole, a disjunction between the whole and space is produced—thus, these occur in one and the same moment.

8.11: Then, at the very moment that the cognition of generality (*sāmānya-buddhi*) arises, at that same moment, due to the destruction of the conjunction that initiates the substance, there is the destruction of the aggregate (*piṇḍa*); and from the destruction of the aggregate, there is the destruction of the conjunction with the aggregate. Subsequently, simultaneously with the cognition of the quality (*guṇa-buddhi*), due to the destruction of the aggregate, the [cognition of] direction, and the conjunction with the aggregate, there is the destruction of "remoteness" (*paratva*).

8.11: How [is this] also due to the simultaneous destruction of the conjunction and the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*)? When "remoteness" (*paratva*) arises, at that time there is motion in the substratum of remoteness. Then, at the very same moment that the cognition of the generality (*sāmānya*) of remoteness arises, the disjunction between the direction and the object is produced by the motion of the object. Thereafter, from the cognition of the generality, the relative cognition is destroyed; and from the disjunction, the conjunction between the direction and the object is destroyed—this constitutes one single moment.
8.11: Subsequently, from the destruction of the conjunction and the relative cognition, the destruction of remoteness occurs.

8.11: How [is it] also due to the simultaneous destruction of the three causes—the inherent, the non-inherent, and the efficient? When the cognition of relative distance (*apekṣābuddhi*) arises, at that time there is motion in the constituent part of the whole; then, at the very same moment that the motion produces a disjunction from another part and the production of "priority" (*paratva*) from the cognition of relative distance, at that same moment there is also motion in the whole. Then, from the disjunction of the parts, the destruction of the conjunction that originated the whole occurs; and by the motion of the whole, a disjunction from space is produced, as well as the production of the cognition of the universal (*sāmānyabuddhi*). Thus, all this occurs at one and the same time.

8.11: Then, from the destruction of the conjunction [of the self and the soul], there is the destruction of the mass; from the disjunction, there is the destruction of the conjunction between the direction and the mass; and from the cognition of the universal [priority], there is the destruction of the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*). Thus, all this occurs simultaneously through the destruction of the three causes—the inherent, the non-inherent, and the instrumental—resulting in the destruction of "remoteness" (*paratva*).
8.12: Intellect (buddhi), apprehension (upalabdhi), knowledge (jñāna), and cognition (pratyaya) are synonyms.
And that [speech] has many varieties because of the infinity of objects and because it is restricted to each specific object.

8.12: Although it is of many kinds, that [cognition] is briefly of two types: knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*). Among these, ignorance is fourfold, characterized by doubt, error, non-determination, and dreaming.

8.12.1.1: Doubt (*saṃśaya*) is, first of all, a deliberation (*vimarṣa*) that relies upon both possibilities, characterized by the thought "What could this be?", arising from the perception of mere similarity between two well-known particulars, the recollection of their respective specific qualities, and the influence of past demerit (*adharma*).

It is of two kinds: internal (*antar*) and external (*bahiḥ*). Internal doubt occurs, for instance, when an instructor, having first pointed out something correctly or incorrectly, points it out again; at that time, a doubt arises regarding the three periods [of past, present, and future] as to whether it was indeed correct or incorrect. External doubt is of two kinds: concerning an object of perception (*pratyakṣa-viṣaya*) and concerning an object beyond perception (*apratyakṣa-viṣaya*).

8.12.1.1: Among these, first, with regard to an object that is not perceptible, doubt arises from the perception of a common mark, the recollection of both specific features, and [the influence of] *adharma*; for example, upon seeing only a horn in a forest, one wonders whether it is a cow or a *gavaya*.

8.12.1.1: Even regarding an object that is not within the range of direct perception, when one observes the mere similarity of height between a post and a person, and due to the non-perception of specific features such as curvature, there is no manifestation of the specific universals such as "post-ness"; then, because both specific features are being remembered, the cognition of the self, being drawn toward both, wavers: "Could this indeed be a post, or could it be a person?"
8.12.1.2: Error (*viparyaya*) also has as its object only that which falls within the scope of perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*).

Regarding the object of perception first: error is the cognition "that is this" with respect to what is not that, arising from the contact of the self and the mind, dependent upon a mental impression produced by a cognition of an object not present due to the improper observation of two well-known particulars by one whose sense organs are afflicted by bile (*pitta*), phlegm (*kapha*), or wind (*anila*), and [caused] by demerit (*adharma*).

8.12.1.2: Just as in the case of "a horse is like a cow," there arises a conceit of perception even when perception is absent, such as when one thinks, "the nocturnal darkness is like the surface of a motionless ocean from which the mass of clouds has departed, dark as a heap of powdered collyrium.
8.12.1.2: Even regarding the object of inference, there is inference of fire by means of what is mistaken for smoke—such as steam—and the cognition of a "cow" upon seeing the horns of a *gavaya*.

8.12.1.2: Erroneous cognition (*viparyaya*) consists of the false conviction that "this is the highest good" regarding the doctrines of the Śākyas and others, which are contrary to the vision of the Triple Veda (*trayī-darśana*); the conceit of self-identity with the body, senses, and mind; the perception of permanence in things that are produced; the knowledge that an effect arises despite the deficiency of its causes; the knowledge that what is taught as beneficial is harmful; and the knowledge that what is taught as harmful is beneficial.

8.12.1.3: Indeterminate cognition (*anadhyavasāya*) also arises only with respect to the objects of perception and inference. Among these, regarding the object of perception, indeterminate cognition is merely a state of wondering, "What is this? arising due to distraction or lack of familiarity, whether the object is well-known or unknown. For example, a person from the Vāhīka region may have such an indeterminate cognition regarding *panasa* (jackfruit) trees and the like. In that case, there occurs a determinate cognition (*adhyavasāya*) based on [the observation of] existence, substantiality, earthness, treeness, possession of color, and so forth, as well as the branches and other features.

8.12.1.3: Even the property of being a *panasa* (jackfruit tree), which persists in all *panasa* trees and is excluded from mangoes (*āmra*) and other species, is indeed directly perceived; however, due to the absence of instruction, there is no comprehension of its specific name.

Furthermore, even regarding an object of inference, a resident of Nārikela-dvīpa (Cocoanut Island) experiences indecision upon seeing only a dewlap, thinking, "What kind of living being could this possibly be?"

8.12.1.4: When one whose collection of sense-faculties has ceased and whose mind has dissolved [from the body] experiences through the very door of the senses that which is mental, that is dream-cognition. How so?

8.12.1.4: When, for the sake of rest at night or for the sake of digesting food, the minds of living beings exhausted by the daytime activities of the self’s body—which are preceded by volition—remain motionless within the heart-region (antarhṛdaya), a part of the self devoid of sense-faculties, due to a continuous flow of activity in the mind based on a connection between the self and the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) and depending on effort induced by the unseen force (adṛṣṭa), then one is designated as "one whose mind has dissolved."

8.12.1.4: When that [waking state] has dissolved, the collection of the sense organs becomes inactive. In that state, while the continuity of the flow of *prāṇa* and *apāna* persists, dream-cognition arises through the door of the sense organs—even though the objects are not present—taking the form of perception due to a specific conjunction of the self and the mind and from the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) known as sleep. That [dream-cognition] is of three kinds: from the intensity of latent impressions, from the imbalance of the bodily humors (*dhātu-doṣa*), and from unseen destiny (*adṛṣṭa*).

8.12.1.4: In that regard, first, due to the proficiency of mental formations (*saṃskāra*), when one who is lustful or angry falls asleep while contemplating some object, then that very stream of thought arises in the form of a direct perception (*pratyakṣākāra*).

Or, due to an imbalance of the elements (*dhātudoṣa*): one of a wind-nature (*vātaprakṛti*) or one afflicted by wind sees such things as traveling through the sky; one of a bile-nature (*pittaprakṛti*) or one afflicted by bile sees such things as entering fire or mountains of gold;
one of a phlegm-nature (*śleṣmaprakṛti*) or one afflicted by phlegm sees such things as crossing rivers and oceans or snow-covered mountains.

8.12.1.4: Regarding things experienced by oneself or not experienced, whether they be well-known objects or unknown objects, whatever indicates auspiciousness—such as mounting an elephant or obtaining a parasol—all that arises from both *saṃskāra* (mental impressions) and *dharma* (merit). Conversely, whatever is the opposite—such as being anointed with oil or mounting a donkey or a camel—all that arises from *adharma* (demerit) and *saṃskāra*.
In the case of extremely unknown objects, it arises solely from the *adṛṣṭa* (the unseen force).

8.12.1.4: Although dream-consciousness occurs when the collection of sense-faculties has ceased, it is nonetheless nothing but memory because it consists in the reviewing of a past continuum of cognition; thus, this constitutes the fourfold ignorance.
8.12.2: Knowledge is also fourfold, characterized as direct perception, inference, recollection, and revelation.
8.12.2.1: In that regard, perception (*pratyakṣa*) arises depending upon each respective sense-organ (*akṣa*). [5: That which arises depending [upon something] is perception.

8.12.2.1: The sense-organs (*indriya*) are six: the nose, tongue, eye, skin, ear, and mind. For that [perception] arises with respect to categories of objects such as substance (*dravya*) and so forth.

8.12.2.1: First, regarding substance, there is a mere observation of the essential form (*svarūpālocanamātra*) when there is a fourfold contact involving magnitude, possession of multiple substances, the manifestation of color-form, and light, along with the totality of conditions such as merit (*dharma*) and so forth.

8.12.2.1: Perception arises from the contact of the self and the mind, depending on qualifiers such as generality, particularity, substance, quality, and action; for example: "the substance exists," "it is earth," "it has horns," "it is white," or "the cow is walking.

Regarding color, taste, smell, and touch, perception arises through the specific sense organ as its cause, due to their inherence in multiple substances, their own inherent particularities, and contact with their own substrates. By that [specific sense organ] alone is there apprehension.

Number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, viscidity, fluidity, speed, and action are perceived by the eyes and the sense of touch because they are inherent in substances that are themselves perceptible.

(8.12.2.1) Cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort are apprehended through the conjunction of both the self and the mind. Properties such as existence, substantiality, quality-ness, and action-ness—which are inherent in their substrata that are themselves objects of perception—are apprehended by those same sense organs that perceive their supports; this is the nature of perception for persons such as ourselves.

8.12.2.1: However, for yogins who are superior to us and are absorbed in yoga, there arises through the mind assisted by dharma born of yoga an unerring perception of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) in their own self, in other selves, in space, direction, time, atoms, air, and minds, as well as in the qualities, actions, universals, and ultimate particulars inherent in them, and in inherence (*samavāya*).

Furthermore, for those who are not absorbed in yoga (*viyukta*), direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of subtle, concealed, or distant objects arises due to the contact of the four factors, through the power of the assistance of dharma born of yoga.

8.12.2.1: In that regard, with respect to universals and particulars, perception (*pratyakṣa*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consisting merely in the observation of the thing's own nature (*svarūpa*). The objects of cognition (*prameya*) are the categories (*padārtha*) such as substance (*dravya*) and so forth. The result of the act of cognition (*pramiti*) is the knowledge whose object is substance and the other categories.

When the knowledge of a universal or a particular arises, perception is the means of valid cognition consisting in an undifferentiated, mere observation; there is no other separate means of valid cognition in this case, because [any such other] would lack the form of a fruit (*aphalarūpatvāt*).

8.12.2.1: Alternatively, that cognition which arises with respect to all objects through the fourfold contact—being non-erroneous and non-verbal—is the means of valid perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*). The objects of knowledge (*prameya*) are the categories (*padārtha*) such as substance and the rest; the knower (*pramātṛ*) is the self (*ātman*); and the resulting knowledge (*pramiti*) is the observation of qualities, defects, or neutrality.
8.12.2.2: That which arises from the observation of a mark is inferential (laiṅgika).

8.12.2.2: Furthermore, the logical mark (*liṅga*) is that which is connected with the object to be inferred (*anumeya*), which is well-known to exist in what possesses that [object], and which absolutely does not exist in the absence of that [object]; such is the inferential mark.
8.12.2.2: That which is the opposite of this—whether by one or by two [of the three characteristics]—Kāśyapa declared to be a non-reason (*aliṅga*), being contradictory, unestablished, or doubtful.

8.12.2.2: That which is concomitant with the object to be inferred (anumeya) in a particular place or at a particular time, which is well-known in another instance—whether in its entirety or in a single part—that possesses the property to be inferred, and which is known through valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) to be absolutely non-existent in every instance contrary to the object to be inferred; that is the mark (*liṅga*) which brings about the inference of an otherwise unknown object.

8.12.2.2: The rule is that where there is smoke, there is fire; in the absence of fire, smoke also does not exist. Thus, for one who has established the convention [of this relationship], from the perception of unambiguous smoke and the recollection of its concomitance (*sāhacarya*), there immediately follows the certain determination (*adhyavasāya*) of fire.

8.12.2.2: In this way, in all cases, that which is inseparably connected with a particular place or time is the mark (*liṅga*) of the other. The mention of "effect" (*kārya*) and so forth in the treatise is made for the sake of illustration, not for the sake of restriction. Why? Because inference arises from the observation of even a single instance.

8.12.2.2: For example, when the *adhvaryu* priest calls for the response "Oṃ śrauṣaṭ," it serves as an indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the *hotṛ* priest who is out of sight; the rising of the moon is an indicative mark of the swelling of the ocean and the blooming of the night-lotuses; and the clarity of the water in autumn is an indicative mark of the rising of the star Agastya.

All such instances are established by the mere statement of a relationship in the form "this belongs to that. Furthermore, that [inference] is of two kinds: that based on what is perceived (*dṛṣṭa*) and that based on general observation (*sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa*).
