8.12.2.2: Among these, *dṛṣṭa* (perceived) inference occurs when there is no absolute difference in genus between the known instance and the object to be proven (*sādhya*). For example, having perceived the mere dewlap in a cow, one recognizes it as a cow upon seeing the mere dewlap again in another place.

8.12.2.2: *Sāmānyato dṛṣṭa* (inference from general observation) occurs when there is an absolute difference in genus between the known instance and the object to be proven, based on the persistence of the commonality of the property of the mark (*liṅga*) and the property to be inferred (*anumeya-dharma*).

8.12.2.2: Just as one observes that the activities of farmers, merchants, and royal officials are productive of results, so too is there an inference of results for those belonging to the [four] castes and [four] stages of life who engage in activity even without aiming at a visible purpose.

In this regard, the perception of the mark (*liṅga*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and the resulting knowledge of fire is the valid cognition (*pramiti*). Alternatively, the knowledge of fire itself is the means of valid cognition, while the observation of the qualities, defects, or neutrality regarding the fire is the valid cognition; such is inference for the sake of determining an object for oneself. 8.12.2.2.A: Verbal testimony and the other means of knowledge are also included within inference, because they function according to the same principle.

8.12.2.2.A: Just as inference regarding a supersensuous object occurs for one who knows the established convention through the perception of an unambiguous mark and the recollection of its established connection, so too does it occur from words and other means of knowledge.

8.12.2.2.A: Even the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) characterized by *śruti* and *smṛti* depends upon the authority of its speaker; the authority of the tradition arises from his word, and because of the inferential mark (*liṅga*), the composition of sentences in the Veda is non-eternal and preceded by conscious intent, since it has been stated that "the act of giving is preceded by conscious intent."
8.12.2.2.A: Since the understanding of one who is familiar with conventional gestures arises from their movement, that too is indeed inference.

8.12.2.2.A: Since an authoritative person conveys the cognition of a gavaya, which is unfamiliar [to the listener], by means of its similarity to a cow, analogy is nothing other than the word of an authoritative person.
8.12.2.2.A: From a perception, there is presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*); from hearing what is contradictory, there is inference based on an inference (*anumitānumāna*).
8.12.2.2.A: Origination, too, is indeed inference because it is invariably concomitant.

8.12.2.2.A: Non-existence (abhāva) is also indeed inference; for example, an effect that has arisen is a mark (liṅga) for the existence of its cause, and likewise, an effect that has not arisen is a mark for the non-existence of its cause.
8.12.2.2.A: Likewise, tradition (aitihya) that is not false is indeed the instruction of a reliable person (āptopadeśa).

8.12.2.2.B: Inference for others (*parārthānumāna*) is the communication of an object ascertained by oneself through a five-membered statement. It should be understood that inference for others is the communication of an object ascertained by oneself to others—those who are doubtful, mistaken, or uninformed—exclusively by means of a five-membered statement.

8.12.2.2.B: Furthermore, the members [of a syllogism] are the proposition (*pratijñā*), the statement of the reason (*apadeśa*), the example (*nidarśana*), the application (*anusandhāna*), and the conclusion (*pratyāmnāya*).
8.12.2.2B1: Among these, the proposition (*pratijñā*) is the enunciation of the object to be inferred (*anumeya*) that is not contradictory.

8.12.2.2B1: A proposition is a mere enunciation intended to bring the subject (*dharmin*), as qualified by the property (*dharma*) one wishes to demonstrate, within the scope of the instruction; for example, "Air is a substance."
8.12.2.2B1: By the inclusion of the term "non-contradictory," those [theses] that contradict perception, inference, accepted scripture, one's own treatise, or one's own words are excluded.

For example: "Fire is not hot" contradicts perception; "The sky is solid" contradicts inference; "Wine may be drunk by a Brahmin" contradicts scripture; for a Vaiśeṣika who asserts that the effect pre-exists in the cause, [the thesis] contradicts his own treatise; and "A word does not convey meaning" contradicts one's own words.

8.12.2.2B2: The indicator (liṅga) is the probans (apadeśa). That which is concomitant with the object to be inferred, which is established by way of generality in all members of its own class, and which is entirely absent in everything contrary to it—that is called the indicator; the statement of that is the probans. For example: "Because of possessing action" and "because of possessing quality. And thus, these [properties] exist in the object to be inferred, and possession of quality exists in all members of its own class, while possession of action exists in some, but not in all.
8.12.2.2B2: Both of these [characteristics] do not exist at all in that which is non-substantial; therefore, it is established that its verbal designation is merely a figurative indication (apadeśa).

8.12.2.2B2: By this, it is stated that the unestablished (*asiddha*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), the doubtful (*sandigdha*), and the non-exclusive (*anadhyavasita*) are not valid reasons (*anapadeśa*). Among these, the unestablished is of four kinds: unestablished for both, unestablished for one or the other, unestablished in its existence, and unestablished with respect to the object of inference (*anumeya*).
Regarding these, "unestablished for both" means it is not established for either the proponent or the opponent, such as: "Sound is impermanent because it possesses parts."

8.12.2.2B2: *Anyatarāsiddha* (unestablished for one of the two parties) is, for example: "Sound is impermanent because it is a product. *Tadbhāvāsiddha* (unestablished in its existence) is, for example: when smoke is presented as the means for the cognition of fire, [that smoke] is unestablished as being smoke if it is actually vapor.

8.12.2.2B2: *Anumeyāsiddha* (unestablished in the subject of inference) is, for example: "Darkness is an earthy substance because it possesses a black color. That which, while not existing in the subject of inference (*anumeya*), does not exist in anything of the same class as that subject, yet exists in what is contrary to it, is *viruddha* (contradictory) because it proves the opposite; for example: "Because it has horns, therefore it is a horse."

8.12.2.2B2: That which exists in the object of inference (*anumeya*) and is common to both similar and dissimilar classes, being indeed present, is "doubtful" (*sandigdha*) because it generates uncertainty—for example: "Because it has horns, therefore it is a cow. Some maintain that this is another type of doubtful reason, because when two reasons possessing the aforementioned characteristics but having contradictory [conclusions] coincide regarding a single subject, doubt is observed;
for example, with respect to whether the mind is corporeal or incorporeal, [the reasons are] its possession of motion and its lack of tangibility.

8.12.2.2B2: But surely this [reason] is indeed uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*), like the properties of being non-visual and being perceptible, because it cannot belong to either of the two sides of the combined [subject]; and therefore we shall state that it is "unconclusive" (*anadhyavasita*). 8.12.2.2B2: But surely it is taught in various places in the treatise that seeing both ways is a cause of doubt; thus, there is no doubt arising from the observation of a duality of objects.

8.12.2.2B2: When doubt arises, the perception of two contradictory objects is the cause; however, if those two were of equal strength, they would fail to produce a definitive conclusion due to their mutual opposition, rather than serving as a cause for doubt. Yet, they do not possess equal strength, because one of the two—the subject of inference—is sublated by scripture (*āgama*). This, therefore, is simply a variety of the "contradictory" (*viruddha*) fallacy. Furthermore, that which exists in the object of inference (*anumeya*) but does not exist in either its similar or dissimilar classes is "unestablished for one of the two parties" (*anyatarāsiddha*); it is called "inconclusive" (*anadhyavasita*) because it serves as a cause for lack of determination. An example is: "The effect pre-exists [in the cause], because it comes into being."
8.12.2.2B2: This is subsumed under the statement that "this is an unestablished non-indicator" (*aprasiddho 'napadeśaḥ*). [Objection:

But has this not been stated as a cause for doubt in the treatise, on the grounds that "a specific feature (*viśeṣa*) is observed in both ways among things of the same class and among those belonging to a different category"? [Response: No, because the word has a different meaning; for a specific feature is observed in the case of sound (*śabda*).

8.12.2.2B2: When it is said that "doubt does not arise," this [audibility] would not be a particularity (*viśeṣa*) of any one of the categories such as substance (*dravya*), but rather it becomes a generality (*sāmānya*) itself. Why? Because it has been stated that among things of the same class and those belonging to different classes—namely, the various divisions of substance and so forth—a particularity is observed in each case in both ways; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of doubt arising even regarding all six categories. Therefore, doubt arises solely from the cognition of a generality.

8.12.2.23: The example (*nidarśana*) is of two kinds: by similarity (*sādharmya*) and by dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). Among these, the demonstration of the concomitance of the general character of the mark (*liṅga-sāmānya*) with the general character of the object to be inferred (*anumeya-sāmānya*) is the example by similarity. For instance: "Whatever possesses activity is seen to be a substance, as for example an arrow. And the demonstration of the absence of the mark in the opposite of the object to be inferred is the example by dissimilarity. For instance: "Whatever is not a substance does not possess activity, as for example existence (*sattā*)."

8.12.2.2B3: By this, fallacious examples (*nidarśanābhāsa*) are excluded. For example: "Sound is eternal because it is incorporeal; whatever is seen to be incorporeal is eternal, such as an atom, such as action, such as a pot, such as darkness, like space," and "whatever is a substance is seen to possess activity. These are fallacious examples by similarity (*sādharmya-nidarśanābhāsa*), being respectively: unestablished in the mark (*liṅga*), the object to be inferred (*anumeya*), or both; unestablished in their substratum (*āśrayāsiddha*); non-concomitant (*ananugata*); and concomitant with the opposite (*viparītānugata*).

8.12.2.2B3: That which is impermanent is seen to be material, such as action (*karman*), such as an atom (*paramāṇu*), such as space (*ākāśa*), and such as darkness (*tamas*). Like a jar, that which is devoid of activity is also non-substantial (*adravya*). These are the fallacious examples of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-nidarśanābhāsa*), characterized respectively by: [the reason] not being excluded from both the probans and the probandum, [the locus] being unestablished, [the reason] not being excluded [from the heterologous], and [the reason] being excluded in the opposite manner.

8.12.2.2B4: *Anusandhāna* (corroboration) is the application of the general mark (*liṅgasāmānya*), which has been observed in the example (*nidarśana*) together with the general property to be inferred (*anumeyasāmānya*), to the object of inference (*anumeya*). 8.12.2.2B4: That statement by which the general mark—conceived as being merely a property of the object of inference, whose capacity [to prove] has not yet been perceived, and which was observed in the example together with the general property to be proven (*sādhyadharmasāmānya*)—is applied to the object of inference, that is *anusandhāna*. For example: "And thus, air possesses motion. 8.12.2.2B4:
And having perceived its absence when the object of inference is absent, one concludes: "But air is not devoid of motion."

The conclusion (*pratyāmnāya*) is the restatement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) for the sake of producing certainty in others regarding that which was indicated as the object of inference but was not yet certain.

The restatement of the proposition (*pratyāmnāya*) is the restatement of the proposition for the sake of producing certainty in others—whose capacities have been stimulated by the members [of the syllogism] such as the reason (*hetu*), etc.—by means of a completed sentence, regarding that which was indicated as the object to be established but was not yet certain; for example: "Therefore, it is indeed a substance."

If it is argued that when this [proposition] is absent, other members—whether taken collectively or individually—lack the capacity to express that meaning because their meaning is already implied, we say no, for this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

To explain: immediately after the proposition, one need only state the reason (*hetu*); since learned persons will recall the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the understanding of its meaning will follow. Therefore, the completion of the purpose occurs right here [in the reason].

By the statement "How is sound impermanent?", sound is described as being qualified merely by an unascertained impermanence; by the statement "because it follows immediately upon effort," the mere property that serves as the means of proving impermanence is expressed;

by the statement "here, whatever follows immediately upon effort is seen to be impermanent, just like a jar," the mere concomitance of the general property of the means of proof with the general property of the probandum is stated;
and by the statement "the eternal is seen not to follow immediately upon effort, just like space," the absence of the means of proof in the case of the absence of the probandum is demonstrated.

And thus, sound is observed to be produced immediately after an effort, whereas it is not the case that sound is not produced immediately after an effort like space; through both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the application of the general property of the probans—whose capacity has been observed—to the specific case of sound is understood. Therefore, by the statement "therefore sound is impermanent," the completion of the intended meaning—that sound is indeed impermanent—is understood. Consequently, it is established that the demonstration of an object ascertained by oneself to others is performed solely by means of a five-membered syllogism; this is what constitutes inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*).

8.12.2.2.C: Ascertainment (*nirṇaya*) is a definitive cognition arising from the perception of specific characteristics that is opposed to doubt. This very [ascertainment] is either perception or inference. 8.12.2.2.C: That which arises from the perception of specific characteristics and is opposed to doubt is perceptual ascertainment (*pratyakṣanirṇaya*).

8.12.2.2.C: Just as, when a doubt arises—such as "Is this a post or a person?"—due to the perception of the mere similarity of height between a post and a person while their specific features remain unperceived, followed by the recollection of the specific features of both; and then, upon seeing the head, hands, and so forth, there arises the determinative knowledge that "this is indeed a person," such determinative knowledge is *pratyakṣa-nirṇaya* (determinate perception).

8.12.2.2.C: Similarly, when a doubt arises—such as "Is this a cow or a gavaya?"—due to the sight of a mere horn, and then, upon seeing the dewlap alone, there arises the determinative knowledge that "this is indeed a cow," such determinative knowledge is *anumāna-nirṇaya* (determinate inference).

8.12.2.3: Memory is that which has past objects as its domain; it is caused by the desire for recollection, the observation of signs, and so forth, arising from a specific conjunction of the self and the mind, and from a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by cognitions characterized by intensity, repetition, or interest, regarding objects seen, heard, or experienced; it is the cause of subsequent determination, desire, recollection, and aversion toward remaining [objects].

8.12.2.4: That knowledge which arises from the conjunction of the self and the mind, due to the specific quality of merit (*dharma*), as an intuitive revelation that reports things as they truly are—concerning objects beyond the senses, whether past, future, or present, such as *dharma* and so forth, whether recorded in texts or not—that is called *ārṣa* (sage-knowledge).
This occurs extensively among divine sages (*devarṣi*) and only occasionally among worldly people, as when a young girl says, "My brother will come tomorrow; my heart tells me so."

8.12.2.5: The vision of the perfected ones (*siddhadarśana*) is not a distinct type of knowledge. Why? Because the vision of those who have attained perfection through ointments, foot-ointments, swords, pills, and so forth—visions that allow them, as seers of the visible, to perceive objects that are subtle, concealed, or distant—is nothing other than perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Furthermore, if it is claimed that there is a vision of the ripening of merit and demerit based on the signs of celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial beings, such as the conjunctions of planets and constellations, that too is simply inference (*anumāna*).

8.12.2.5: Now, if it is maintained that the perception of dharma and so forth is independent of indicative marks (liṅga), even that is included within either perception (pratyakṣa) or the words of a seer (ārṣa); such is the understanding.

8.13: Pleasure is characterized by gratification (*anugraha*). When desired objects such as garlands and the like are present, pleasure arises from the contact of the sense organs with their objects resulting in the perception of what is desirable, and from the conjunction of the self and the mind depending upon merit (*dharma*) and other factors; it is that which produces gratification, attachment, and clarity of the eyes and other faculties. [Pleasure] regarding past objects is born of memory; regarding future objects, it is born of conceptualization (*saṅkalpa*). However, that which manifests for the wise even in the absence of the recollection of objects, desire, or conceptualization, has its cause in knowledge (*vidyā*), tranquility (*śama*), contentment (*santoṣa*), and a specific state of merit (*dharma-viśeṣa*).
8.14: Pain is characterized by affliction.

When there is the presence of undesirable objects such as poison and the like, pain arises from the contact of the sense organs with their objects resulting in the perception of the undesired, depending on demerit (*adharma*) and other factors, due to the conjunction of the self and the mind; it is that which has indignation, affliction, and dejection as its causes.
Regarding past objects such as snakes, tigers, and thieves, it is born of memory; regarding future ones, it is born of imagination (*saṅkalpa*).

8.15: Desire (*icchā*) is the longing for that which has not yet been attained, whether for one's own sake or for the sake of another. It arises from the conjunction of the self and the mind, depending either on pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth, or on memory (*smṛti*). It is the cause of effort (*prayatna*), memory, merit (*dharma*), and demerit (*adharma*). Desire, longing, passion (*rāga*), resolve (*saṅkalpa*), compassion (*kāruṇya*), dispassion (*vairāgya*), hypocrisy (*upadhā*), disposition (*bhāva*), and so forth, are varieties of desire. Sexual desire is *kāma*.

8.15: *Abhilāṣa* is the desire for the wish to consume [food]. *Rāga* is the desire for repeated attachment to sense objects. *Saṅkalpa* is the desire for action that is not yet imminent. *Kāruṇya* is the desire to eliminate the suffering of others without regard for one's own interest. *Vairāgya* is the desire to renounce sense objects due to perceiving their defects. *Upadhā* is the desire to deceive others. *Bhāva* is a desire hidden within. Varieties of desire arise from the differences in actions, such as the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) or the desire to abandon (*jihīrṣā*).

8.16: Hatred (*dveṣa*) consists of a state of burning. That in the presence of which one considers oneself as if set ablaze is hatred. It arises from the conjunction of the self and the mind, depending either upon pain or upon memory.
8.16: It is the cause of effort, memory, merit (*dharma*), and demerit (*adharma*). Anger, malice, resentment, intolerance, and impatience are varieties of hatred.

8.17: *Prayatna* (effort) is synonymous with *saṃrambha* (exertion) and *utsāha* (zeal). It is of two kinds: that preceded by life (*jīvanapūrvaka*) and that preceded by desire and aversion (*icchādveṣapūrvaka*). Among these, the one preceded by life is that which impels the continuous flow of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* breaths in one who is asleep, and at the time of awakening, it is the cause for the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) to reach other sense organs.

This [effort] preceded by life arises from the conjunction of the self and the mind, depending upon merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*). The other [kind of effort], however, is the cause of activity capable of attaining the beneficial and avoiding the harmful, and it is that which sustains the body.
8.17: And that [action] arises from the conjunction of the self and the mind, depending on desire or depending on aversion.

8.18: Heaviness (*gurutva*) is the cause of the action of falling in water and earth. It is imperceptible and is to be inferred from the action of falling. It is opposed by conjunction (*saṃyoga*), effort (*prayatna*), and mental impression (*saṃskāra*). Its eternality, non-eternality, and production are like those of color and other qualities in atoms of water and so forth.

8.19: Fluidity is the cause of the action of flowing. It subsists in three substances. It is of two kinds: natural (*sāṃsiddhika*) and incidental (*naimittika*). Natural fluidity is a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of water; incidental fluidity is a common quality (*sāmānyaguṇa*) of earth and fire. Regarding natural fluidity, its eternality, non-eternality, and production are like those of gravity. If it is argued that natural fluidity is untenable because we observe [earthly] aggregates, [the answer is] no.

8.19: The mutual conjunction of aqueous atoms endowed with divine heat, known as "aggregation" (*saṃghāta*), is the initiator of the substance [snow]. Because of this, the fluidity of the atoms is obstructed; consequently, fluidity does not arise in its effects, such as snow and hail.
Furthermore, the occasional fluidity of earth and fire is produced by conjunction with fire.

8.19: How is it that, when action arises in the atoms—the causes of clarified butter, lac, beeswax, and so forth—due to contact with fire depending on momentum (*vega*), and when, through the disjunctions resulting therefrom, the conjunctions that initiate the substance are destroyed and the effect-substance ceases to exist; then, due to contact with fire depending on heat (*auṣṇya*), fluidity (*dravatva*) arises in those independent atoms? Subsequently, when action arises in them due to contact between the self and the atoms depending on the unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) of experiencers, and when the effect-substance is produced through the sequence of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth from the conjunctions resulting therefrom; at that time, simultaneously with the arising of color and other qualities, fluidity arises in that substance through the sequence of the qualities of the causes. Thus [it is explained].

8.20: Viscidity (sneha) is the specific quality of water; it is the cause of cohesion, lubricity, and so forth. Like gravity, its eternity, non-eternity, and production are likewise [to be understood].

8.21: *Saṃskāra* (impression/disposition) is threefold: velocity (*vega*), mental impression (*bhāvanā*), and elasticity (*sthitisthāpaka*). Among these, velocity arises from action dependent on a specific cause in the five corporeal substances; it is the cause of a continuous series of actions in a fixed direction, is opposed by a specific conjunction with a substance possessing touch, and in some cases arises through a sequence beginning with the qualities of the cause. The mental impression, however, is a quality of the self (*ātman*) which becomes the cause of memory and recognition regarding objects seen, heard, or experienced. It is opposed by knowledge, intoxication, pain, and so forth. A sharp excellence of *saṃskāra* arises from the conjunction of the self and the mind when there is a cognition of a marvelous object that depends upon a sharp cognition [of that object], such as for a Southerner upon seeing a camel. When learning, arts, athletics, and the like are being practiced, an excellence of *saṃskāra* arises from the conjunction of the self and the mind due to each subsequent cognition depending upon the preceding *saṃskāra* regarding that very same object. For one who, having fixed the mind upon the eye with effort, desires to see a previously unseen object, an excellence of *saṃskāra* arises from the conjunction of the self and the mind depending upon a cognition of intense interest (*ādara*), such as from seeing a flash of lightning. Or, as in the case of seeing silver and golden lotuses in the lake of the gods (*devahrada*). Elasticity, however, exists in tangible substances characterized by a dense arrangement of parts and persisting over time; it restores its own substratum to its original state when it has been altered. The effect of elasticity is observed in stationary and moving modifications—such as bows, branches, horns, tusks, bones, threads, and garments—when they are bent or coiled. Regarding its eternity, non-eternity, and production, it is like gravity (*gurutva*).

8.22: *Dharma* is a quality of the person (*puruṣaguṇa*). It is the cause of what is dear, beneficial, and liberation for the agent; it is supersensible (*atīndriya*), and it is opposed to the consciousness of final bliss. It arises from the conjunction of the person and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) when there is a pure intention (*abhisandhi*), and it has specific means prescribed for those belonging to the various classes (*varṇa*) and stages of life (*āśrama*). The means for that [dharma] are substances (*dravya*), qualities (*guṇa*), and actions (*karman*) prescribed by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, existing in the relationship of general and particular for those in the classes and stages of life. Among these, the general means for dharma are: faith in dharma, non-violence, benevolence toward living beings, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, freedom from deceit, avoidance of anger, ritual bathing, the use of prescribed substances, devotion to a specific deity, fasting, and vigilance. For the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, and Vaiśya, [the general duties are] sacrifice (*ijyā*), study (*adhyayana*), and giving (*dāna*). For the Brāhmaṇa, the specific [duties] are receiving gifts (*pratigraha*), teaching (*adhyāpana*), officiating at sacrifices (*yājana*), and the sacraments (*saṃskāra*) prescribed for his own class. For the Kṣatriya, they are the proper protection of subjects, the suppression of the wicked, not retreating in battles, and his own sacraments. For the Vaiśya, they are agriculture, trade, commerce, cattle-rearing, and his own sacraments. For the Śūdra, they are dependence on the preceding classes and performing rites without mantras. As for those in the stages of life: for the student (*brahmacārin*) living in the teacher’s household, they are the duties prescribed by his own scriptures—service to the teacher, gathering fuel for the fire, the practice of begging for alms, and the avoidance of honey, meat, sleeping during the day, collyrium, ointments, and so forth.

8.22: For a householder who has completed his studies and vows (*vidyāvratasnātaka*) and taken a wife, there is the performance of the five great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*)—known as those for beings, humans, gods, ancestors, and Brahman—at morning and evening, using wealth acquired through the *śālīna* or *yāyāvara* modes of livelihood, according to the rules of the single sacred fire (*ekāgni*). When capable, he should also perform the permanent cooked-sacrifice rites (*pākayajñasaṃsthā*), the oblation-sacrifice rites beginning with the establishment of the fires (*agnyādheya*), and the Soma-sacrifice rites beginning with the *agniṣṭoma*. During the intervals between the seasons, he should observe celibacy and procreate offspring. Alternatively, whether he remains a student or a householder, he may depart from the village to dwell in the forest; there he wears bark garments, skins, and keeps his hair, beard, nails, and body hair long. For the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), his food consists of wild offerings, sacrificial remnants, and the leftovers of guests. Finally, for the wandering mendicant (*pravrajita*), who is faithful and has granted perpetual fearlessness to all beings, having renounced his own ritual duties and remaining vigilant in the restraints and observances, the accomplishment of Yoga comes from the discernment of the six categories. These means of accomplishment, performed without aiming at visible results and depending on the clarity of one's disposition, lead to the arising of Dharma from the conjunction of the self and the mind.

8.23: Adharma is also a quality of the self (*ātman*). It is the cause of harm and transgression for the agent, is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), and is opposed to the cognition of final suffering. Its means are those prohibited in the scripture (*śāstra*), which are the opposites of the means of dharma, such as violence, falsehood, theft, and so forth, as well as the non-performance of what is enjoined and negligence. Depending upon these, and upon a corrupt intention, adharma arises from the conjunction of the self and the mind.

8.24: From a predominant dharma that impels one who is ignorant and possessed of passion and hatred, yet accompanied by a small amount of adharma, there arises a conjunction with desirable bodies, senses, objects, pleasures, and so forth, in accordance with one's latent dispositions (*āśaya*), within the worlds of Brahmā, Indra, Prajāpati, the ancestors, and humans. Likewise, from a predominant adharma accompanied by a small amount of dharma, there arises a conjunction with undesirable bodies, senses, objects, and sufferings in the states of existence as hungry ghosts and animals.
8.24: Thus, from dharma characterized by worldly activity when conjoined with adharma, there arises the bondage of saṃsāra again and again among gods, humans, animals, and denizens of hell.

8.24: However, for one who acts preceded by knowledge and without intending a fruit, is born into a pure family, desires to know the means for the cessation of suffering, approaches a teacher, and has produced knowledge of the reality of the six categories—such a person, upon the cessation of ignorance, becomes dispassionate. Due to the absence of passion, hatred, and so forth, there is no production of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), which are conquered by those [passions]. Through the exhaustion of previously accumulated [karma] by experience, contentment and happiness arise, as does the dissolution of the body. Upon the cessation of passion and the like, the solitary *dharma* characterized by cessation, having produced the happiness born from the vision of ultimate reality, ceases. Then, due to that cessation, the mind becomes seedless; there is the cessation of the body and so forth. When there is no further production of the body and so forth, liberation (*mokṣa*) is the subsiding [of all things], like a fire whose fuel is consumed.

8.24: Sound is a quality of space (*ākāśa*); it is perceptible by the sense of hearing; it is momentary; it is opposed both to its cause and its effect; it is produced from conjunction, disjunction, and sound; it exists in specific locations (*pradeśavṛtti*); and it has causes that are both similar and dissimilar. It is of two kinds: characterized as phonemes (*varṇa*) and characterized as resonance (*dhvani*). Among these, the phoneme-characterized [sound] begins with the letter *a* and so forth, while the resonance-characterized [sound] is caused by conch shells and the like. Regarding this, the production of the phoneme-characterized [sound] occurs as follows: from the conjunction of the self and the mind, there arises—dependent upon memory—the desire to utter a phoneme. Immediately following that, an effort (*prayatna*) arises. Dependent upon that effort, an action is produced in the air (*vāyu*) due to the conjunction of the self and the air. That air, moving upward, strikes the throat and other articulatory sites (*sthāna*). Then, dependent upon the conjunction of the articulatory site and the air, the phoneme is produced from the conjunction of the articulatory site and space (*ākāśa*).

8.24: Even though it lacks specific color-characteristics (*avarṇalakṣaṇa*), sound arises from the conjunction of the drum and the space within the drum, depending upon the conjunction of the drumstick and the drum. Furthermore, from the disjunction of the bamboo joints and the disjunction of the bamboo and the space, as well as from the sound produced by conjunction and disjunction, there occurs a series of sounds like a succession of waves. Thus, through this series, the sound reaches the region of the ear and is perceived. Since there is no going or coming of either the ear or the sound, there is no perception of something that has not reached [the sense organ]; therefore, by process of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), the existence of the series is established.
8.0: The section on the category of quality (guṇapadārtha) in the Praśastapādabhāṣya is completed.
The Category of Action (karmapadārtha) 9.0: Now follows the definition of the category of action.

9.1: All five types of action—upward throwing (utkṣepaṇa) and the rest—are related to the category of action (karmatva). Their specific characteristics are: inherence in a single substance; momentariness; subsistence in corporeal substances; possession of no qualities; being produced by gravity, fluidity, effort, or conjunction; opposition to their own effect, which is conjunction; being a cause independent of [other] conjunctions or disjunctions; being a non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa); initiating effects that inhere in themselves and in other substrates; not initiating effects of the same genus; not initiating [new] substances; and possessing a restricted genus. Furthermore, their distinction lies in their initiating effects characterized by spatial direction.

9.2.1: Among these, throwing upward (utkṣepaṇa) is that action which, produced from gravity, effort, and conjunction, occurs in the limbs of the body or in things connected to them, and which is the cause of conjunction with upper regions and the cause of disjunction from lower regions. This is throwing upward.
9.2.1: That action which is the cause of conjunction and disjunction contrary to that [previous one] is throwing upward (apakṣepaṇa).

9.2.2: Contraction (*ākuñcana*) is that action by which, through the separation of the parts at the front of a straight substance from their respective locations and the conjunction of those parts with the regions at the base, the whole (*avayavin*) becomes curved.
9.2.2: By the reverse of that [conjunction], when conjunction and disjunction arise, that action by which the whole becomes straight is extension (*prasāraṇa*).
9.2.3: That which is the cause of conjunctions and disjunctions in an indefinite direction and location is motion.

9.3: This fivefold action, existing in the limbs of the body and in things connected to them, is either with a cause (*sapratyaya*) or without a cause (*apratyaya*); that which is other than these is indeed without a cause (*apratyaya*), and their movement consists in [action] toward those others. It is incorrect to say that actions are of only five types, because there is no distinction in their being "movement. For every momentary action, having arisen as mere movement, produces conjunctions and disjunctions with points of space—whether upward, downward, or horizontal—even by the measure of an atom; thus, the cognition of "movement" remains constant everywhere, and therefore everything is simply movement. [Response: No, because we observe the recurrence and exclusion of cognitions according to classes. Here [we perceive] "lifting," elsewhere "lowering," and so on; since the recurrence and exclusion of cognitions are observed everywhere according to classes, a distinction between universals and particulars (*sāmānya-viśeṣa-bheda*) is understood as the cause thereof. Furthermore, due to the specific prefixes such as *ud-* and others, and because they initiate effects characterized by specific directions, a distinction in their defining characteristics (*upalakṣaṇa-bheda*) is also established. Even so, the restriction that there are "only five" is untenable, because even in cases such as "going out" (*niṣkrāmaṇa*) and "entering" (*praveśana*), we observe the recurrence and exclusion of cognitions according to classes. If you maintain that a distinction of genus (*jāti-bheda*) is desired in the case of lifting and so forth because we observe the recurrence and exclusion of cognitions according to classes everywhere, then the same would apply to going out, entering, and so on. If you argue that the recurrence and exclusion of cognitions in those cases arise from a difference in the effect (*kārya-bheda*), we say no; for then it would follow that the recurrence and exclusion of cognitions in lifting and so forth also arise merely from a difference in the effect. Alternatively, if you claim that while the recurrence and exclusion of cognitions according to classes exist equally [in both sets], there is a specific reason why the distinction of genus applies only to lifting and so forth and not to going out and so forth, we say no, because this leads to the undesirable consequence of a confusion of genera (*jāti-saṅkara*). If the recurrence and exclusion of cognitions in going out and so forth were due to a distinction of genus, a confusion of genera would result. How so? When two observers simultaneously perceive the cognitions of "going out" and "entering" as one person moves from one room to another, or when at the doorway one perceives "he enters" and "he goes out"; yet when the curtain or door is removed, there is neither the cognition of entering nor the cognition of going out, but only the cognition of "movement. Similarly, when a bamboo leaf or the like falls into a tube, many observers simultaneously perceive the cognitions of "whirling," "falling," and "entering"—thus, there is the undesirable consequence of a confusion of genera. Such a confusion of cognitions is not observed in the case of lifting and so forth; therefore, the recurrence and exclusion of cognitions in lifting and so forth are due to a distinction of genus, whereas in going out and so forth they are due to a difference in the effect. If you ask, "How can there be a simultaneous difference in cognitions? Suppose you think: "Just as there is no confusion of genera, there is also no co-inherence of multiple actions; how then do the cognitions of whirling, falling, and entering occur simultaneously regarding a single action? To this we reply: No, because of the difference between the parts and the whole, and the difference between the conjunctions and disjunctions characterized by specific directions.

9.3: For one who perceives the conjunctions and disjunctions of the parts with the various spatial directions in succession from the side, there arises the cognition of "turning. For one who observes the disjunction from the upper region and the conjunction with the lower region in the whole (avayavin), there arises the cognition of "falling. Furthermore, for one who perceives the conjunction within the interior space and the disjunction in the exterior space, there arises the cognition of "entering. Thus, it is established that the difference in cognitions regarding exiting and so forth results from the difference in their effects. Let it be granted that the difference in cognitions regarding upward-thrusting and so forth arises from a difference in their generic classes (jāti); however, the difference in cognitions regarding exiting and so forth arises from a difference in their effects.

9.3: Now, is "going-ness" (*gamanatva*) a synonym for "action-ness" (*karmatva*), or is it a distinct universal (*sāmānya*)? From what source does this doubt arise? It is understood that it is a synonym for "action-ness" because, just as there is the cognition of "action" in those [four types of action] beginning with upward throwing (*utkṣepaṇa*), there is no difference in the cognition of "going" across them all. However, since it is designated by a specific name like upward throwing and so on, it might therefore be a distinct universal. [Reply: No, because it is a synonym for "action-ness. Just as "selfhood" (*ātmatva*) and "personhood" (*puruṣatva*) are synonyms, "going-ness" is indeed a synonym for "action-ness. [Objection: For what purpose was the term "going" included by means of a specific designation? [Reply: It is not for the sake of excluding whirling (*bhramaṇa*) and so forth; rather, the inclusion of "going" was made in order to include whirling, falling (*patana*), vibrating (*spandana*), and the like, which are not already encompassed by the terms "upward throwing" and so on. Otherwise, it would follow that only those four which were mentioned by specific names would be the objects of the general and specific designations. Alternatively, let "going-ness" be a distinct universal that resides only in whirling and so forth, which cause conjunctions and disjunctions in indefinite directions; and the word "going" should be regarded as applied figuratively (*bhākta*) to upward throwing and the rest, due to the commonality of being the agent of conjunctions and disjunctions with respect to its own substratum.

9.4: The rule for action based on cognition (*sat-pratyaya-karma-vidhi*). How does it occur? When one desires to perform sacrifices, Vedic study, giving, agriculture, and so forth, and wishes to raise up or lower down the hand, then an effort (*prayatna*) arises in that part of the self (*ātman*) where the hand is located. Due to that effort and by disregarding gravity (*gurutva*), action occurs in the hand from the conjunction of the self and the hand. As with the hand, this applies to all limbs of the body, such as the feet, and to the body itself. How does it occur even in those things connected [to the body]? When, having grasped a pestle with the hand, one forms the desire, "I shall raise up the pestle with my hand," immediately thereafter an effort arises. From the conjunction of the self and the hand, disregarding that effort, at the very same time that the action of raising up arises in the hand, at that same time, from the conjunction of the hand and the pestle, disregarding that very same effort, action also arises in the pestle.

9.4: When the pestle has been thrown upward to a great distance, the desire for that [upward] purpose ceases; then, once again, the desire to throw it downward arises. Immediately following that, from the aforementioned conjunction of the hand and the pestle—which depends upon that effort—two simultaneous actions of throwing downward occur. Then, by means of the final action of the pestle, a conjunction called "impact" (*abhighāta*) is produced between the mortar and the pestle. That conjunction, depending upon the momentum residing in the pestle, produces an action of upward flight in the pestle even in the absence of an external cause (*apratyaya*). That action, depending upon the impact, initiates a latent disposition (*saṃskāra*) in the pestle. Depending upon that [disposition], the conjunction of the hand and the pestle produces an action of upward flight in the hand as well, even though there is no [external] cause. Even if the previous disposition has perished, nevertheless, because the conjunction of the pestle and the mortar is a specific kind of conjunction capable of producing a potent action, it is able to assist in the initiation of that new disposition. Alternatively, the very same potent disposition from before remains undestroyed due to the impact. Therefore, since there is no initiation of a further disposition in what already possesses a disposition, at the very moment when the action of upward flight occurs in the pestle without an external cause due to the impact depending on the disposition, at that same moment, an action of upward flight also occurs in the hand without an external cause, depending upon that very same disposition and the conjunction of the hand and the pestle.

9.4: The procedure for throwing among those [actions] involving a stake (*paṇi*). How is it? When a desire arises to throw a stake after grasping it with the hand, immediately thereafter an effort (*prayatna*) arises. In dependence upon that [effort], from the two aforementioned conjunctions (*saṃyoga*), simultaneous actions of drawing toward oneself arise in both the stake and the hand. When the hand has been extended, the effort intended for drawing it back ceases. Immediately thereafter, a desire arises, "I shall throw [it] sideways, upwards, far away, or near. Immediately thereafter, an effort corresponding to that [desire] arises. In dependence upon that [effort], the conjunction between the stake and the hand, called "impulsion" (*nodana*), arises. From that, an action arises in the stake; depending on that impulsion, it initiates a momentum (*saṃskāra*) within it. Then, by means of both the momentum and the impulsion, actions continue to occur as long as there is no separation between the hand and the stake. Thereafter, when the impulsion has ceased due to that separation, actions corresponding to the [original] effort—whether upwards, sideways, far, or near—occur by virtue of the momentum until the falling [of the stake].

9.4: Likewise, regarding the mechanism [of the bow], this is the method of motion as described. How so? A strong man who has practiced exercise, having steadied the bow with his left hand, fixed an arrow with his right, and grasped the string together with the arrow in his fist, forms the desire to draw it, thinking, "I shall draw this strung bow. Immediately thereafter, when an action of drawing arises in the hand due to the contact between the self and the hand—which depends upon that effort—then, at that very moment, an action arises in the string and the arrow due to the contact between the hand, the string, and the arrow, which depends upon that same effort. Furthermore, two actions arise in the two ends of the bow due to the contacts between the string and the ends of the bow, which depend upon the specific contact between the hand, the string, and the arrow. All of this occurs simultaneously. Thus, when the bow is drawn back to the ear, there arises the cognition that "it need not be drawn further than this"; from that, the effort for the purpose of drawing ceases. Then, the desire to release [the arrow] arises. Immediately thereafter, an action occurs in the fingers due to the contact between the self and the fingers, which depends upon that [new] effort. From that, there is a separation between the string and the fingers; from that separation, the contact [between them] is destroyed. When that contact is destroyed, because of the absence of an obstacle, the *sthitisthāpaka* (elasticity) inherent in the bow causes the bow, which had become circular, to return to its original state. At that time, an action arises in the string and the arrow due to the contact between the bow and the string, which depends upon that very elasticity. That action produces an elasticity (*saṃskāra*) in the string depending upon its own cause. Depending upon that [elasticity], the contact between the arrow and the string becomes a *nodana* (impulse). From that impulse, an initial action is produced in the arrow; depending upon that impulse, it initiates an elasticity within the arrow.

9.4: Therefore, actions arise from the *saṃskāra* (impulse) aided by the *nodana* (initial impulsion) for as long as there is the separation of the arrow from the bowstring; once the *nodana* has ceased due to that separation, subsequent actions occur solely from the *saṃskāra* residing in the arrow until its fall. Why are there many actions in succession? Because there is a multiplicity of conjunctions (*saṃyoga*). However, the *saṃskāra* is singular, because in the interval between actions there is no further causal factor (*apekṣākāraṇa*) [to produce another].

9.4: Thus, action based on a real cause and action based on an unreal cause have been explained with respect to things presided over by a self. 9.5: In external things not presided over by a self, action consisting solely of motion arises from causes such as impulsion (*nodana*) and so forth, which lack a [real] cause [in the form of a self]. In that regard, impulsion is a particular kind of conjunction which, depending upon gravity, fluidity, momentum, and effort—either collectively or individually—is the cause of a single action that brings about non-separation; from that, action occurs in all four great elements (*mahābhūta*).

9.5: As in the case of earth known as mud (*paṅka*). Impact (*abhighāta*) is that specific conjunction, dependent on velocity, which is the cause of a single action that results in disjunction. From that also, action occurs in the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), as when hard objects such as stones fall upon it; likewise, when earth known as mud is pushed by feet or the like, or is struck, there is a conjunction—dependent on either pushing or impact, or on both—which is a "conjunction with what is conjoined" (*saṃyukta-saṃyoga*). From that also, action occurs in earth and the other elements. Furthermore, action is produced even in those parts that are neither pushed nor struck. Falling (*patana*) is the downward motion due to gravity (*gurutva*) when there is an absence of gravity-supporting conjunction, effort, or velocity, as described in the case of a pestle, the body, and so forth. Among these, the first [action] is from gravity, while the second and subsequent ones are from gravity and momentum (*saṃskāra*).

9.5: The downward flow of water, which has become a stream, from high ground to low ground is due to its fluidity (*dravatva*). How so? When the fluidity of the whole (*avayavin*) is obstructed on all sides by contact with a dam, the fluidity of the parts (*avayava*), which inheres in the same object as that [whole], is likewise obstructed by that very same [dam]. Furthermore, the fluidities of each successive part are obstructed by the conjunctions of those [parts] in contact with one another. However, when a breach is made in the dam to a certain extent, because the fluidity of the whole is obstructed on all sides, there is no initiation of the effect [of flow]; yet, for the fluidity of the part situated near the dam, and for the fluidities of the successive parts, there is the attainment of their function (*vṛttilābha*) due to the absence of an obstructing factor. Consequently, there is a gradual downward movement of those very [parts] in contact. Then, upon the destruction of the previous substance, a long substance is initiated by the parts remaining in a continuous series. In that case, fluidity arises through the sequence beginning with the qualities of the causes. And when the causes in contact move in a continuous series, the action (*karman*) that arises in the whole is called "flow" (*syandana*).

9.5: Action resulting from *saṃskāra* (elasticity/disposition) has been explained in the case of arrows and the like. Similarly, when parts [of an object] such as a wheel produce conjunctions and disjunctions with specific directions and locations on their sides, that action of the whole which—caused by *saṃskāra*—is the cause of conjunctions and disjunctions with non-specific directions and locations, is called "revolution" (*bhramaṇa*). Such are the various types of motion.

9.5: Regarding the action in the wind called *prāṇa*, it arises from the conjunction of the self and the wind, depending on an effort preceded by desire or aversion; for in the case of one who is awake, we observe conformity to desire, whereas in the case of one who is asleep, it depends on an effort preceded by the mere impulse to live. As for ether (*ākāśa*), time (*kāla*), direction (*dik*), and the self (*ātman*), although they possess substantiality, they are devoid of action because they are incorporeal (*amūrtatva*), like universals (*sāmānya*) and the rest. Corporeality (*mūrti*) is the dimension of a non-omnipresent substance, and action conforms to that [corporeality]; since that [corporeality] does not exist in ether and the others, there is no connection with action for them.

9.5: When the mind possesses a body, the action of a waking person for the purpose of connecting with another sense organ arises from the conjunction of the self and the mind, depending on an effort preceded by desire and aversion; this is because we observe the perception of other objects through different sense organs according to one's intention. At the time of awakening for one who has slept, it depends on an effort preceded by the life-force (*jīvana*). Furthermore, the action of departing (*apasarpaṇa*) and the action of entering (*utpasarpaṇa*) arise from the conjunction of the self and the mind, depending on the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*). How so? When there is the exhaustion or mutual suppression of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), which are the auxiliaries of the life-force due to their experience [of results], then, because of the deficiency of those two which assist the life-force, there is a deficiency in the effort preceded by them. Upon the cessation of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), the action of departing—which causes separation from the dead body—arises from the other two, merit and demerit, which have acquired their functional state and are assisted by the conjunction of the self and the mind.

9.5: Then, having departed from the body, [the self] becomes connected with a subtle body (*ativāhika-śarīra*) produced by those very same *dharma* and *adharma*. Transferred by that [subtle body], it goes to heaven or hell and becomes connected with a body corresponding to its latent dispositions (*āśaya*). For the sake of that conjunction, there is the approach of *karma*. And for yogis, there is the departure of the mind projected externally to a desired place and its return. Likewise, at the time of creation (*sarga*), there is the action caused by the unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) for the sake of connection with a new body. Similarly, whatever else among the gross elements has no perceptible or inferable cause but is capable of providing benefit or harm, that too is caused by the unseen. For example: the action of atoms at the beginning of creation; the upward and horizontal movement of fire and air; the agitation of the gross elements; the movement of consecrated gems toward a thief; and the attraction of iron toward a magnet.
9.0: Thus ends the category of action (*karma*) in the *Praśastapādabhāṣya*.
The Category of Generality (sāmānyapadārtha) 10.0: Now follows the definition of the category of generality.

10. Universality (*sāmānya*) is twofold: the higher (*para*) and the lower (*apara*). It pervades its own entire domain, possesses a non-different nature, and subsists in many individuals. It produces the cognition that follows the essential form of itself across one, two, or many [individuals], and it exists as a continuous presence in its substrata through its non-differentiation from their own forms; thus, it is the cause of the cognition of recurrence (*anuvṛtti*). How so? Because, when a cognition arises continuously with respect to each individual object by depending on the universal, and because of the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by the cognition of repetition, there is a reflection upon the continuity of past cognitions; that which is pervasive therein is the universal. Among these, the higher universal is existence (*sattā*), which is solely the cause of the cognition of recurrence. Just as in the case of mutually distinct objects such as leather, cloth, and woolen blankets, there is a recurrence of the cognition "blue, blue" due to the connection with a single substance, *nila* (the quality of blueness), so too in the case of mutually distinct substances, qualities, and actions, there is a recurrence of the cognition "existent, existent" due to the undifferentiated *sattā*. And since this [recurrence] must arise from something other than the objects themselves, that which is the "other thing" is established as *sattā* (existence).

10. Because it is connected with existence (*sattā*), there is the recurrence of the cognition "existent, existent"; therefore, that [existence] is indeed a universal (*sāmānya*). Other [universals], such as substantiality (*dravyatva*), quality-ness (*guṇatva*), and action-ness (*karmatva*), are both universals and particulars (*viśeṣa*) because they are the causes of both recurrence and exclusion. Among these, substantiality is a universal because it is the cause of recurrence among earth and the other substances which are mutually distinct, and it is a particular because it is the cause of exclusion from qualities and actions. Likewise, quality-ness is a universal because it is the cause of recurrence among color and the other qualities which are mutually distinct, and it is a particular because it is the cause of exclusion from substances and actions. Similarly, action-ness is a universal because it is the cause of the recurring cognition among upward throwing and the other actions which are mutually distinct, and it is a particular because it is the cause of exclusion from substances and qualities. In this way, for earth-ness, color-ness, upward-throwing-ness, cow-ness, jar-ness, cloth-ness, and so forth—whether residing in living beings or non-living things—the state of being both universal and particular is established because they are the causes of recurrence and exclusion. However, these [universals] beginning with substantiality are primarily universals because their scope is extensive; they are designated as "particulars" figuratively because they differentiate their own substrates.

10. Due to the difference in their defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), it is established that these [universals] are distinct categories (*padārtha*) from substance, quality, and action. For this very reason, they are eternal. They are distinct from one another because of the restriction of their occurrence within substances and so forth, and because of the difference in their cognitions. Each universal is a single entity because its defining characteristic is non-distinct throughout its own substrates, and because there is no further particularizing characteristic (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*). Although universals have unlimited spatial extension, they nevertheless pervade all of their own objects due to the restriction of their indicators (*upalakṣaṇa*) and the restriction of the causal complex (*kāraṇa-sāmagrī*). Furthermore, in the intervals between them, they are not designated as such because of the absence of the modes of relation known as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and inherence (*samavāya*).
10.0: Thus ends the category of generality (sāmānya) in the Praśastapādabhāṣya.
The Category of Particularity (viśeṣapadārtha) 11.0: Now follows the definition of the category of particularity.

11. Those existing in the ultimate [entities] are the *antyāḥ* (ultimate); they are called *viśeṣāḥ* (particularities) because they distinguish their own substrata. They reside one by one in each eternal substance—which is devoid of destruction or origination—namely, atoms, ether, time, space, self, and mind. They are the causes of the cognition of absolute differentiation. Just as for people like us, a differentiation of cognition based on common form, quality, action, and the conjunction of parts is observed in cows and the like when distinguished from horses and the like—as in "cow," "white," "swift-moving," "thick-humped," or "large-bellied"—so too, for yogins who are superior to us, there exists among eternal atoms and liberated selves and minds—which possess identical forms, qualities, and actions—a differentiation of cognition such as "this is distinct" and "this is distinct," occurring in each respective substratum. Since no other cause is possible, those causes from which this differentiation of cognition arises, and through which recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) occurs even when atoms are remote in space and time, thinking "this is that very same atom," are the ultimate particularities (*antyā viśeṣāḥ*).

11: Furthermore, if there were a differentiation of cognition and recognition among yogins arising from the dharma born of yoga (*yogaja-dharma*) without [the existence of] ultimate particularities (*antyaviśeṣa*), what would follow? It is not the case that such a thing occurs. Just as from the dharma born of yoga, a cognition of "white" does not arise regarding something that is not white, nor does recognition occur regarding something never before seen; if it were to occur, it would be erroneous. Likewise, here too, without ultimate particularities, neither the differentiation of cognition nor recognition can arise for yogins from the dharma born of yoga. If it is asked: "Why is it not postulated that the differentiation of cognition occurs intrinsically (*svataḥ*) in atoms, just as it does in ultimate particularities?"—we say no, because of identity (*tādātmya*). In this world, with respect to things that do not possess that nature, a cognition arises due to another cause, as in the case of jars and the like [being perceived] by means of a lamp, but not in the case of a lamp [being perceived] by means of another lamp. Just as the impurity of cows, horses, meat, and so forth is intrinsic, while in other things it exists through association with them, so too here, due to identity, the differentiation of cognition occurs intrinsically in ultimate particularities, and through association with them, in atoms and the like.
11.0: Thus ends the category of particularity (viśeṣa) in the Praśastapādabhāṣya.
The Category of Inherence (Samavāya):
Now follows the definition of the category of inherence.

12: Inherence (*samavāya*) is that relationship between things that are inseparably established (*ayutasiddha*), which exist as the supported and the support, and which is the cause of the cognition "it is here. It is the relationship called inherence from which there arises, with respect to substances, qualities, motions, universals, and particulars—whether they stand in a causal relation or not—the cognition "this is here" regarding those things that are inseparably established and exist in the state of being the supported and the support; and it is that from which non-separation (*aviṣvagbhāva*) occurs among non-pervasive things whose distinctness has been apprehended. How so? Just as the cognition "curd is in this bowl" is seen to occur when a relationship exists, so too are there observed such cognitions as: "the cloth is in these threads," "the mat is in these *vīraṇa* grasses," "quality and motion are in this substance," "existence (*sattā*) is in this substance, quality, or motion," "substance-ness (*dravyatva*) is in this substance," "quality-ness (*guṇatva*) is in this quality," "motion-ness (*karmatva*) is in this motion," and "ultimate particularities (*antyā viśeṣāḥ*) are in this eternal substance. From the observation of these cognitions, it is known that a relationship exists between them.

12. Nor is this a conjunction (*saṃyoga*), because the related entities are not established as inseparable (*ayutasiddha*), because the causes such as the action of one of the two are impossible, because no end in disjunction (*vibhāga*) is observed, and because there exists only the relationship between the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) and that which is located therein (*adhikartavya*).

12. And that [inherence] is a distinct category from substance and the others, just like existence (*bhāva*), because its defining characteristic is different. Just as existence, substanceness, and so forth, are distinct entities from their own substrates and from one another—because they produce cognitions corresponding to their own nature in their respective substrates—so too inherence is a distinct category from those [five categories], because the cognition "it is here" is observed in the five categories. Nor is it manifold like conjunction, because its indicative mark is non-distinct from that of existence and because there is no specific indicative mark [for plurality]; therefore, like existence, inherence is one everywhere.

12. [Objection: But if inherence (*samavāya*) is one, then because it is a single relation with respect to substances, qualities, and actions as well as qualifiers such as "substanceness" (*dravyatva*), "qualitiness" (*guṇatva*), and "actionness" (*karmatva*), there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of a confusion of categories (*padārtha-saṅkara*). [Reply: No, because of the restriction between the locus (*ādhāra*) and the located (*ādheya*). Even though inherence is one and independent everywhere, there nonetheless exists a restriction between the locus and the located. How so? Why is it that substanceness occurs only in substances, qualitiness only in qualities, and actionness only in actions? This and so forth [is explained] from the observation of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Because of the observation of the positive concomitance of the cognition whose cause is inherence—namely, the cognition "here [it is]"—it is understood that inherence is one everywhere. Because of the observation of the negative concomitance of the causes of [cognitions] such as "substanceness," the specific restriction is known. Just as, despite the oneness of the conjunction (*saṃyoga*) between a bowl and curd, there is a restriction regarding the relationship of locus and located; likewise, even though inherence is one for substanceness and the rest, there is a restriction of locus and located due to the difference in the powers of the manifested (*vyaṅgya*) and the manifestor (*vyañjaka*).

12. Even though the relation is eternal, it is not non-eternal like conjunction, because, like existence (*bhāva*), it is without cause. Just as it has been stated that existence is eternal because no cause for it is perceived through any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), so too is inherence (*samavāya*). For no cause whatsoever for this [inherence] is perceived through any means of valid cognition. But by what kind of subsistence (*vṛtti*) does inherence reside in substances and the other categories? Conjunction is not possible, because conjunction, being a quality (*guṇa*), must reside in a substance. Nor is inherence itself [the mode of subsistence], because it is unitary, and there is no other mode of subsistence. [Reply: No, because it is of the nature of identity (*tādātmya*). Just as for substances, qualities, and actions—which are of the nature of existence (*sattā*)—there is no further connection with existence; likewise, for inherence, which is indivisible and consists of the very nature of subsistence, there is no other subsistence. Therefore, its subsistence is within its own self.

12: For this very reason, inherence is beyond the senses, because it does not function within perceptible objects—just as [qualities] such as existence (sattā) do not—and because there is no self-referential awareness of it. Therefore, inherence is to be inferred from the cognition of "here" (ihabuddhi).
12.0: Thus ends the category of inherence in the Praśastapādabhāṣya.
Salutation to Kaṇabhuj, who, having pleased Maheśvara through the power of his yogic practice, composed the Vaiśeṣika treatise.
Thus ends the commentary on the six categories, beginning with substance, composed by Praśastapāda.
